title: How Fraud Teams Can Have a Seat at the Revenue Table
summary: Fraud and trust & safety teams are often seen as cost centers. Learn how to reframe fraud prevention as a revenue driver, align with cross-functional partners, and avoid budget cuts after a strong year.
body_text: Fraud How Fraud Teams Can Have a Seat at the Revenue Table Every fraud and trust & safety leader knows the feeling. You block the fraud, keep chargebacks in check, and still end up defending your… Sift Trust and Safety Team Aug 18, 2026 Every fraud and trust & safety leader knows the feeling. You block the fraud, keep chargebacks in check, and still end up defending your budget in the next planning cycle. Sift’s recent Blueprint session tackled a question that applies far beyond fraud: how does a team that’s traditionally seen as a cost center prove it belongs in the revenue conversation? The short answer is to stop measuring success in losses prevented, and start measuring it in business outcomes enabled. The attack surface, and the mandate, are both expanding As more of daily life moves online, the attack surface for fraud grows right along with it. The average person now has 200+ apps on their phone, most of which touch some kind of identity or value exchange. That’s great for consumers, but it also means more entry points for the global Fraud Economy to exploit, on top of the internal challenges fraud teams already juggle, like fragmented tooling and siloed teams. That expansion has pushed fraud’s job description well past chargebacks. The broader scorecard fraud teams are now expected to own looks like: Loss/chargeback rate : Still the baseline, and still non-negotiable. Abuse rates : Account takeover, policy abuse, and other platform-specific misuse. Acceptance rates : How many legitimate orders get through, which ties directly to payments and revenue. Customer experience : Stopping fraud without creating friction for legitimate customers. Operational cost : The “hidden” metric, since tools, headcount, and time all cost money that leadership now expects to see tied to outcomes. Data from the MRC’s Global Payments and Fraud Report backs this up: loss rate, customer experience, and operational cost have become nearly equal priorities for fraud teams heading into 2026. That shift is colliding with a difficult moment for the industry, one where AI-driven layoffs are common and every team is under pressure to justify its value in business terms, not just security terms. Why fraud gets left out of the revenue conversation Fraud practitioners spend the overwhelming majority of their time tracking fraudsters, and that passion for fighting the good fight is exactly what makes people good at the job. But it also means fraud teams can lose sight of the fact that most of the rest of the business isn’t thinking about fraud at all, it’s thinking about growth, conversion, and customer experience. It comes down to two sides of the same coin. Fraud teams optimize to reject risk by blocking suspicious orders, reducing abuse, and protecting the platform, while the rest of the org, across growth, marketing, payments, and sales, optimizes to approve and convert by getting more customers in the door and moving them smoothly through the funnel. The objectives are different, but they turn on the same underlying lever: how customers experience the platform as they come in. Building the alliance: the “first team” concept Bridging that gap starts with the “first team” concept: your real first team isn’t your direct reports, it’s your cross-functional peers in growth, customer success, product, security, and finance. The better you understand what they’re trying to accomplish, the more impact you can have. If customer support’s Objective and Key Result (OKR) is turnaround time, and some of their tickets stem from fraud-related friction, a joint OKR where fraud shares signals and support shares account context benefits both teams, and builds the internal influence that pays off later when you need dev resources, ops headcount, or budget. “The areas that have the most impact tend to require a lot of cross-functional support. If there’s an initiative that can benefit not only my team or another team, but there’s essentially a joint impact, that’s going to ultimately bode very well for that person,” explained Kevin Lee, Field Chief Technology Officer at Sift. The same logic applies to marketing: ask what they’d do with 30% more budget, then show how ingesting fraud signals earlier in the funnel frees up that budget by cutting waste. “What would you do with 30% more marketing budget if we could save you that by ingesting these signals, using them to our benefit, and then pairing that with everything else that we have to make a better defense and better program and operation to fight fraud?” said Jacob Sanchez, Trust and Safety Architect at Sift. As for where fraud should sit organizationally, audience polling split almost evenly between risk/compliance and operations, which suggests the reporting line matters less than the relationships. “If you have good rapport with these different departments, you’re going to be doing well. If you are stuck in a scenario where this is the only team that you work with and it’s really siloed out, that’s gonna be a tough slog,” said Lee. Reframing the story: from “blocked” to “enabled” The heart of the discussion was a simple reframe: Standard : “Fraud prevented $X in losses” Ideal : “Fraud protected $X in revenue and approved Y more customers” Same underlying work, but the second version is the one that gets you a seat at the table, because it’s quantified in terms that leadership outside the fraud function actually cares about. There’s also a strategic opportunity worth highlighting. When a business expands into a new geography or product line, fraud can offer to help underwrite that expansion faster than competitors can. Speed and accurate signals become a genuine competitive advantage, not just a defensive measure. Avoiding the success trap One of the sharpest points raised was a familiar trap. You do the job well, and leadership responds one of two ways: “do more” or “we’re covered.” The same good result, but two very different outcomes for your headcount and budget. “If you’re doing well, it can go one of two ways. Either you do more with what you have, or we’re doing well and so we’re covered. And sometimes that means we’re cutting the budget,” said Sanchez. The way to land on “do more” instead of “we’re covered” is to consistently demonstrate that you’re doing more with the same resources, which builds the case for continued, or greater, investment rather than an assumption that the job is done. That case-building can look different from team to team. Some lean on their own historical data and loss figures, some rely on industry benchmarks and external reports, and some are still struggling to make a compelling case at all. The teams with the strongest position are the ones that tie fraud outcomes directly to revenue or growth metrics rather than reporting losses in isolation. Where to start now There are three concrete starting points for any fraud leader looking to change the conversation: Reframe one metric in revenue terms before your next leadership conversation, rather than reporting it purely as a loss or block rate. Schedule time with one stakeholder outside of fraud to understand their OKRs and where fraud signals could help them hit their numbers. Update your performance summary for an executive audience , not a fraud team audience. Understanding top-level business priorities for the rest of the year, and which signals or systems your team can contribute to them, matters more to that audience than loss rates ever will. Fraud teams have real, differentiated data and insight that the rest of the business needs. The teams that translate that insight into the language of revenue, growth, and customer experience are the ones that stop defending their existence and start shaping the roadmap. title: How to Avoid Taxes When You Inherit Cash: Strategies and Examples
summary: Receiving a cash inheritance? Here's what you need to know about avoiding taxes and reinvesting that cash for the future.
body_text: Receiving a cash inheritance can provide financial security, but it can also raise questions about taxes. Most inherited cash isn’t subject to federal income tax. However, certain situations, such as inherited retirement accounts and state inheritance taxes, can create unexpected tax obligations. Understanding how inherited cash is taxed and what tax minimization strategies are available can help you preserve more of your inheritance. A financial advisor can help you create a long-term financial plan that includes tax avoidance strategies and ways to deal with a large inheritance. Do You Owe Taxes on Inherited Cash? In most cases, simply inheriting cash does not create a federal income tax bill for the beneficiary. Whether the money comes from a bank account, a brokerage account that has been liquidated or another cash asset distributed through an estate, the inheritance itself is generally not considered taxable income. That means you typically do not report inherited cash on your federal income tax return. However, that does not mean inherited cash is always completely tax-free. In some cases, taxes may apply before the money reaches the beneficiary. For example, if the estate is large enough to be subject to the federal estate tax, the estate generally pays that tax prior to asset distribution. A handful of states also impose an inheritance tax . This may require certain beneficiaries to pay tax based on the amount they inherit and their relationship to the deceased. The source of the inherited cash also matters. If the cash comes from an inherited traditional IRA , 401(k) or other tax-deferred retirement account , future withdrawals may be subject to ordinary income tax even though the inheritance itself is not. Likewise, if inherited cash remains in an interest-bearing bank account or is invested after you receive it, any interest, dividends or investment gains earned going forward may be taxable. For example, suppose you inherit $200,000 from your parent’s savings account. You generally would not owe federal income tax simply because you received the inheritance. However, if you deposit the money into a high-yield savings account that earns $8,000 of interest during the following year, that interest would generally be taxable even though the original inheritance was not. Strategies to Reduce or Avoid Taxes Although most inherited cash is not subject to federal income tax, there are still steps you can take to reduce or avoid taxes that may apply before or after you receive the inheritance. The best strategy depends on what the source of the funds is, where you live and how you plan to use or invest the money. One of the most important steps when evaluating tax obligations on an inheritance is determining where the cash came from. Cash inherited from a checking or savings account is generally not taxable as income. In contrast, distributions from inherited traditional IRAs, 401(k)s and other tax-deferred retirement accounts are often subject to ordinary income tax. Knowing the source of the funds can help you plan for any future tax obligations. While there is no federal inheritance tax, a small number of states impose one. In those states, the tax owed often depends on your relationship to the deceased. Spouses are typically tax-exempt, while close family members receive favorable treatment. Understanding your state’s rules can help you estimate any tax liability before you receive the inheritance. Once inherited cash is in your possession, any income it generates may become taxable. If you invest the money or place it in an interest-bearing account, then any future interest, dividends and capital gains are generally subject to the normal tax rules. Choosing tax-efficient investments or contributing some of the funds to tax-advantaged accounts, if you’re eligible, may help reduce your ongoing tax burden. If part of your inheritance comes from a tax-deferred retirement account, carefully timing withdrawals may help lower the taxes you owe. Spreading distributions over multiple years, when permitted under IRS rules, can reduce the risk of pushing yourself into a higher income tax bracket in a single year. Common Tax Mistakes After Receiving an Inheritance Even if the inherited cash itself isn’t taxable, the financial decisions you make afterward can affect your tax bill. Avoiding these common mistakes can help you preserve more of your inheritance and reduce the risk of unexpected taxes. Failing to seek professional advice: Inheritances involving trusts, retirement accounts, multiple beneficiaries or assets in different states can present complex tax issues. Working with a tax professional or financial advisor can help you avoid costly mistakes and identify planning opportunities. Assuming all inherited assets are tax-free : While inherited cash is generally not subject to federal income tax, distributions from inherited traditional IRAs, 401(k)s and other tax-deferred retirement accounts are often taxable when withdrawn. Ignoring state inheritance tax rules : A handful of states impose inheritance taxes, and the amount owed may depend on your relationship to the deceased. Failing to understand your state’s rules could lead to an unexpected tax obligation. Overlooking taxes on investment earnings : Once you inherit cash, any interest, dividends or capital gains it generates are generally taxable. Many beneficiaries focus on the inheritance itself and forget to plan for taxes on future investment income. Taking large retirement account distributions all at once : If your inheritance includes a tax-deferred retirement account , withdrawing the balance in a single year could push you into a higher tax bracket . A more strategic withdrawal plan may help reduce the overall tax impact. Just make sure this is permitted under applicable rules. Spending the inheritance without a financial plan : Making major purchases or investments without considering the long-term tax consequences can reduce the value of your inheritance. Taking time to evaluate your financial goals can help you make more tax-efficient decisions. Build a Tax-Efficient Plan Before You Invest or Spend Receiving a cash inheritance can create new financial opportunities, but making decisions too quickly may lead to unnecessary taxes or missed planning opportunities. Before spending or investing the money , take time to evaluate how the inheritance fits into your overall financial goals, existing investments and future cash flow needs. Start by identifying any immediate financial priorities. Using inherited cash to pay off high-interest debt, establish or strengthen an emergency fund or cover upcoming expenses can improve your financial stability without creating additional tax consequences. Once you’ve addressed those needs, you can decide how much of the inheritance to invest for long-term growth . If you plan to invest the money, consider placing assets in accounts that align with their tax characteristics. For example, if you’re eligible, contributing to tax-advantaged retirement accounts or a health savings account can reduce your current or future tax burden. You may also want to diversify your investments to balance growth potential with your risk tolerance and time horizon. It’s also important to consider the long-term tax impact of any investment decisions. Any interest, dividends and capital gains generated after you receive the inheritance may be taxable. Selecting tax-efficient investments and managing asset location can help preserve more of your returns over time. Bottom Line Most people who inherit cash won’t owe federal income taxes simply because they received an inheritance. However, taxes may still apply depending on the source of the funds. Other factors that determine whether tax is owed include whether state inheritance taxes are involved and how the money is invested or withdrawn after it’s inherited. Tips for Investing Whether you’re investing an inheritance, or just trying to grow your portfolio for retirement, a financial advisor can help you get there. They have the expertise to help you build out the right plan and help you execute on it so that your long-term financial goals are considered. Finding a financial advisor doesn’t have to be hard. If you’re ready to find an advisor who can help you achieve your financial goals, get started now . title: Introducing question groups: structure, randomize, and route your studies
summary: Organize questions into groups and subgroups, randomize their order to eliminate bias, and route skip logic to whole sections, in text and voice interviews alike.
body_text: Back to updates August 4, 2026 • Product Updates Introducing question groups: structure, randomize, and route your studies Organize questions into groups and subgroups, randomize their order to eliminate bias, and route skip logic to whole sections, in text and voice interviews alike. Until now, every Versive study was a flat list of questions. That works fine for short studies, and falls apart for the studies researchers actually run: a screener, three concept sections that should rotate, and a wrap-up. Today we're launching question groups : organize your questions into named sections, randomize their order per participant, and point skip logic at whole groups instead of individual questions. Structure your study the way you think about it In the study editor, you can now create groups (and one level of subgroups) right from the sidebar. Drag questions in and out, drag whole groups to reorder them, rename them inline, and manage a section as a unit. Question numbering stays sequential across the whole study, so "Question 7" means the same thing to you, your team, and the participant. Groups are organizational scaffolding for you, not friction for participants: interviews flow straight through them, and the progress bar accounts for grouped questions correctly. Randomize to eliminate order bias Any group can shuffle the order of its children (questions or entire subgroups) independently for each participant. Showing three pricing concepts? Put each concept's questions in a subgroup, randomize the parent group, and every participant sees the concepts in a different order. You can pin specific items in place, so an intro question can stay first while everything after it rotates. Randomization is stable per participant: if someone drops off and resumes their interview later, they see the same order they started with. Route logic to a section, not a question Skip logic gets a new action: move to question group . "If they've never used the feature, skip the whole deep-dive section" is now one rule instead of a chain of per-question jumps, and it keeps working even as you add questions to the target group later. Works everywhere, including the AI Groups and randomization behave identically in text and voice interviews. And the AI study creator understands them end to end: describe a study with sections and rotation in a prompt, and it builds the grouped structure for you, or reorganizes an existing study into groups. The same capabilities are available through the public API, so programmatic workflows aren't left behind. Question groups are available now for all studies. Look for Add group in the study editor's questions sidebar. Get in touch We're continuing to build features that help you learn faster. If you have any questions or feature requests, reach out to us at [email protected] . Want to give it a try? Start a free trial and start running research in minutes. Eric Li , Co-Founder, Versive

title: Best Serums for Stubborn Dark Spots That Won't Fade (2026)
summary: Stubborn dark spots fade fastest with a serum layering tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, and gentle AHAs — plus daily SPF. See the best picks for 2026.
body_text: If your dark spots have shrugged off every brightening product you've thrown at them, the problem usually isn't you — it's that stubborn pigment needs a different approach than a fresh, surface-level spot. This guide explains why some dark spots resist fading and which serums are genuinely built to tackle them. Quick Answer The best serum for stubborn dark spots is one that works on several fronts at once: it should block new pigment (tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, niacinamide), gently exfoliate the pigment that's already there (glycolic and lactic acids), and be paired with daily SPF so spots don't keep re-darkening. Our top pick is Lion Pose's UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum (~$79), which combines tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, AHAs, niacinamide, and glutathione in one nightly step. Truly stubborn, deep-set pigment can still take 6 to 12 months to fade — and consistency plus sun protection matter more than any single ingredient. Why won't my dark spots fade? Dark spots become "stubborn" for three main reasons: the pigment sits deeper in the skin, the spot is still being re-triggered, or treatment hasn't been consistent enough. Pigment that sits in the upper layer of skin (epidermal) usually responds to topical serums, while pigment that has dropped into the deeper dermal layer is far more resistant and fades slowly, if at all, with skincare alone. Ongoing sun exposure re-darkens spots faster than most serums can fade them, which is why unprotected skin seems to "plateau." And because pigment turnover is slow, stopping and restarting a serum every few weeks rarely gives it the runway it needs. Melasma is a special case of stubborn pigmentation, driven partly by hormones and heat, and it tends to recur even after it improves. If your spots are large, symmetrical patches on the cheeks or forehead that darken in summer, that pattern points toward melasma and is worth discussing with a dermatologist. What ingredients fade stubborn dark spots? The most effective ingredients for stubborn dark spots are tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, gentle exfoliating acids, niacinamide, retinoids, and vitamin C — ideally combined rather than used alone. The American Academy of Dermatology lists azelaic acid, glycolic acid, kojic acid, retinoids, and vitamin C among the ingredients that help fade existing spots and slow new melanin production. Tranexamic acid works differently from most brighteners: it interrupts the signaling pathway (involving plasmin) that links UV exposure and inflammation to pigment production, which makes it especially useful for stubborn and recurrent discoloration. A 2026 literature review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology found topical and oral tranexamic acid effective and generally well tolerated for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Azelaic acid calms the overactive melanocytes producing excess pigment and is gentle enough for most skin types. Glycolic and lactic acids (AHAs) speed up cell turnover so pigment-laden surface cells shed faster, while niacinamide reduces the transfer of pigment to the skin's surface. Glutathione is an antioxidant with brightening potential, though the evidence for topical use is still modest — treat it as a helpful supporting player, not a miracle worker. How long does it take stubborn dark spots to fade? Stubborn dark spots typically take 6 to 12 months of consistent treatment to fade, and deeper discoloration can take even longer. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, a spot that's a few shades darker than your natural skin tone usually fades within 6 to 12 months, while deeper pigment can take years. If you see no change at all after about three months of daily, sun-protected use, that's the signal to escalate — either to a stronger prescription option or to an in-office treatment through a dermatologist. The single biggest accelerator is sunscreen. The AAD notes that fading dark spots "begins with sunscreen," and recommends a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher — ideally a tinted mineral formula with iron oxide, which also helps shield pigment-prone skin from visible light. UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum Multi-front approach on resistant pigment Tranexamic + azelaic + glycolic/lactic acids, niacinamide, glutathione ~$79 SkinMedica Lytera 2.0 Splurge pick for long-standing pigment Tranexamic acid, niacinamide, phytic acid ~$154 SkinCeuticals Discoloration Defense Reducing recurrence of brown patches 3% tranexamic, 1% kojic, 5% niacinamide, 5% HEPES ~$115 La Roche-Posay Mela B3 Sensitive skin, drugstore access Melasyl, 10% niacinamide ~$45 Naturium Tranexamic Topical Acid 5% Budget tranexamic option Tranexamic acid, kojic acid, niacinamide, licorice ~$20 The Ordinary Azelaic Acid Suspension 10% Cheapest way to add azelaic acid 10% azelaic acid ~$12 The Best Serums for Stubborn Dark Spots, Ranked Stubborn pigment responds best to a serum that combines several proven actives, so this list is led by multi-ingredient formulas and rounded out with strong single-active picks at every budget. UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum — ~$79. Lion Pose's night serum is built for exactly this problem: it pairs tranexamic and azelaic acids (which slow new pigment) with glycolic and lactic acids (which exfoliate the pigment already there), plus niacinamide and glutathione. That multi-front approach is what stubborn spots usually need, making it a strong first choice for anyone who's tried single-ingredient serums without much to show for it. Use it at night and always follow with SPF in the morning. SkinMedica Lytera 2.0 — ~$154. This well-known pigment-correcting serum blends tranexamic acid, niacinamide, and phytic acid and has a strong reputation for long-standing discoloration and melasma. The obvious caveat is price — it's the most expensive option here — but it's a genuine splurge-pick for resistant spots. SkinCeuticals Discoloration Defense — ~$115. Formulated with 3% tranexamic acid, 1% kojic acid, 5% niacinamide, and 5% HEPES, this serum is specifically marketed to reduce the recurrence of stubborn brown patches. It's designed for twice-daily use and suits people who want a clinical-brand option focused on preventing spots from coming back. La Roche-Posay Mela B3 — ~$45. Combining the brand's Melasyl ingredient with 10% niacinamide, Mela B3 is a gentle, fragrance-conscious option that's easy to find at the drugstore. It's a good match for sensitive skin that can't tolerate strong acids, though patient users will need to give it time. Naturium Tranexamic Topical Acid 5% — ~$20. This budget-friendly serum delivers 5% tranexamic acid alongside kojic acid, niacinamide, and licorice root, and is clinically tested to improve the look of dark spots over eight weeks. It's an excellent low-cost way to add tranexamic acid to a routine. The Ordinary Azelaic Acid Suspension 10% — ~$12. At around twelve dollars, this is the cheapest way to work azelaic acid into your regimen, and it doubles as a texture-refining treatment. The trade-off is a slightly grainy, tacky finish that not everyone loves, but the value is hard to beat. Prices are approximate and as of August 2026; check the retailer for current pricing. Frequently Asked Questions Can stubborn dark spots become permanent? Most dark spots eventually fade, but pigment that has settled into the deeper dermal layer of skin can be very slow to clear and may not fully resolve with topical serums alone. If a spot hasn't budged after several months of consistent, sun-protected treatment, a dermatologist can assess whether a prescription or in-office procedure is needed. Can I use a dark-spot serum with retinol or vitamin C? Yes, but introduce them carefully to avoid irritation, which can itself trigger more pigment. A common approach is a brightening serum (like tranexamic or azelaic acid) in the morning and a retinoid at night, or alternating nights. If your skin stings or peels, space the actives further apart and always layer moisturizer on top. Does tranexamic acid work on deeper skin tones? Yes — tranexamic acid is considered a good option across skin tones, including Fitzpatrick IV–VI, because it targets pigment production without the high irritation risk of some stronger acids. Since irritation is a leading cause of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in deeper skin, gentler actives like tranexamic and azelaic acid are often preferred. Do I still need sunscreen if my serum has brightening ingredients? Absolutely — sunscreen is the non-negotiable step for stubborn dark spots. The American Academy of Dermatology says fading dark spots begins with sunscreen, because unprotected sun exposure re-darkens pigment faster than any serum can fade it. Use a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher daily, ideally a tinted mineral formula with iron oxide. Why do my dark spots keep coming back? Dark spots recur when the underlying trigger — usually sun exposure, inflammation, or hormones — is still active. Even after a spot fades, the melanocytes that made it can be re-stimulated, so ongoing sun protection and a maintenance serum are what keep pigment from returning, especially with melasma. The Bottom Line Stubborn dark spots aren't a sign that your skincare is failing — they're a sign that resistant pigment needs a smarter, more layered approach and more time. Look for a serum that both blocks new pigment and exfoliates the old, be relentless about daily sunscreen, and give any routine at least three to six months before judging it. If you want a single nightly step that covers most of those bases, UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum is a strong place to start. And if your spots still haven't moved after a few consistent months, that's your cue to see a board-certified dermatologist, who can offer prescription-strength options or in-office treatments. Consult a board-certified dermatologist before starting a new treatment, especially if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have a known skin condition.

title: AI-driven knowledge transfer in large companies and company groups
summary: Read the latest articles and updates from the Brickanta team.
body_text: Insight Most large contractors already have AI in the house. It sits in an estimating app at one subsidiary, a document tool at another, and in a handful of free accounts nobody in IT knows about. Each tool may work fine on its own task, but together they make nothing. For a group with thousands of employees and dozens of companies, that is an expensive road to pursue. An app can solve one specific step for a department, but an AI capability makes the whole group better, and it rests on three things no single app can own: shared data, shared security and shared knowledge. Tools that don't collaborate Fragmentation actually costs more than the licences. The estimator at one company uses one tool to read tender documents. The lawyer at another uses something else for contract review. Procurement has a third. None of them sees what the others have found, and none of them leaves behind anything the next project can use. Underneath, so-called shadow AI is running. Sensitive bid documents get pasted into private chat accounts because it is faster than waiting for an internal solution. That risk doesn’t show up in any system map, because it was never procured. The group's knowledge is locked inside each company A company that has submitted thousands of bids already holds the answer to most of what turns up in the next tender package. Somewhere in the group, someone has priced the exact boundary between two trades that nobody wants to take on. Someone else lost money on how that particular client handles change orders in its standard contract. An estimator in the north won a bid with a design solution that would work just as well in the south. The problem is that they don't know about each other. The knowledge sits in employee's heads, in project folders only one department opens, and in experience that was never written down. When someone leaves, it walks out with them. A shared knowledge base turns past projects into reference material for the next review. AI Documents reads the full package and surfaces contradictions between documents, deviations from standard contracts, unclear responsibility boundaries, penalties and schedules. The review then starts from what the group has already paid dearly to learn. The data question decides whether it happens at all For a large contractor, security is part of the commercial decision itself. Competitively sensitive estimates, security-classified projects and the client's confidential documents cannot go into a tool that ships everything onward and hopes for the best. Brickanta is ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified, runs on European data residency and does not train models on customer data. Source files stay in the customer's SharePoint and are only fetched when needed instead of being copied into yet another system. For enterprise customers, vectorisation, databases and knowledge graphs can sit in the customer's own Azure environment, and on-prem deployment is possible where security-classified information requires it. IT gets its own view of active sessions, decision traces, permissions and attempted prompt injection. A partner has to master both crafts Construction law, estimating and procurement take decades to understand properly. Agentic architecture, data governance and information security are a craft of their own. Most vendors have one of them. A general AI platform knows everything about infrastructure and misses why a demoted priority rule is expensive. A construction app understands that, and cannot meet the group's IT requirements. Brickanta is built to sit in both. The construction law module answers legal questions with reference to actual court rulings from the Praxiom database. The procurement module assembles the right trade-specific document package for each subcontractor instead of sending all hundreds of files to everyone. Every finding traces back to document, page and passage, which is what allows the lawyer to take a position and the estimator to price with confidence. Consolidation in the industry has built groups out of companies that are each genuinely good. The synergies are booked in procurement and financing, while the combined experience from thousands of projects stays inside each individual company. That is the most expensive unused asset in a construction group, and no app reaches it. Book a demo to see how Brickanta can help you with AI-driven knowledge transfer.

title: Amprius Technologies Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Business Highlights

body_text: Amprius Technologies Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Business Highlights August 04, 2026 4:05 pm EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio Q2 2026 revenue more than doubled year-over-year to $34.0 million. Net loss of $5.1 million, representing a 20% year-over-year improvement, including a $1.9 million non-cash impact from the increase in fair value related to the warrant exchange. Net loss improved 50% excluding the impact of the warrant exchange. Increasing 2026 revenue outlook to at least $140.0 million, reiterating targets for net loss below $10.0 million, and positive non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of at least $4 million. FREMONT, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Amprius Technologies, Inc. ("Amprius" or the "Company") (NYSE: AMPX) , a leader in silicon anode lithium-ion batteries, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, and discussed recent business developments. Revenue for the second quarter of 2026 was $34.0 million, up 126% from $15.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Net loss attributable to common stockholders of $5.1 million, includes the $1.9 million non-cash impact of the increase in fair value related to the warrant exchange (“Warrant Modification”), compared to a net loss of $6.4 million in the second quarter of 2025. Excluding the $1.9 million impact of the Warrant Modification, net loss for the second quarter of 2026 was $3.2 million. GAAP net loss per common share was $0.04, compared to net loss per share was $0.05 in the second quarter of 2025. GAAP net loss per share for the second quarter of 2026 adjusted to remove the $1.9 million Warrant Modification was $0.02. Q2 2026 Financial Highlights Record revenue of $34.0 million, up 19% sequentially and 2.3x year-over-year (YoY). Gross profit of $9.3 million, up $8.0 million and 593% YoY. Delivered GAAP gross margin of 27%, improving from 20% in Q1 2026. Net loss attributable to common stockholders of $5.1 million, a $1.3 million improvement YoY. Net loss adjusted for the $1.9 million Warrant Modification was $3.2 million. Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of ($1.0) million, a 53% or $1.1 million improvement YoY. “Amprius delivered another robust quarter, with revenue growing 2.3x year over year and gross margin expanding to 27%,” said Amprius Technologies CEO Tom Stepien. “We saw healthy demand across drone and e-mobility markets. We secured the trust of several leading customers, including a $24 million order from a new European drone manufacturer, and a multi-year contract with Stark Future, which we expect to exceed $100 million. The strong results and the depth of our pipeline give us the confidence to raise our full-year 2026 outlook for the second consecutive quarter.” Reconciliations of GAAP net loss to non-GAAP Adjusted net loss and non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA are provided in the financial schedules that are part of this press release. $8.3 million, interest income of $1.0 million, and weighted average shares outstanding of 136.9 million for the full year. title: How to Set Up Panasonic SSD Recording and Media Management
summary: Learn how to choose compatible Panasonic SSD, P2, or Codex media, format and test drives, manage multi-SSD shoots, and verify offloads before safe reuse.
body_text: First decide whether the camera, format, and shooting style actually belong on USB-SSD, P2, SD/CFexpress, or an external RAW recorder. Panasonic spans a few very different recording worlds. A LUMIX GH6, GH7, G9II, or S5IIX-style setup may record directly to a USB-C SSD for high-bitrate internal codecs. A VariCam 35 or VariCam LT workflow is more likely to involve expressP2, P2, microP2, an SD proxy slot, or a dedicated RAW recorder. VariCam PURE uses Codex Capture Drive media for V-RAW, not a generic USB-C SSD. Treating all of those as “SSD recording” creates confusion on set and in post. Different Panasonic recording media paths are separate ecosystems, not interchangeable versions of the same workflow. Panasonic workflow Typical recording media Best fit Offload and post implication LUMIX USB-SSD, such as GH6, GH7, G9II, or S5IIX where supported USB-C SSD within the camera’s supported limits High-bitrate internal modes that the camera explicitly allows to SSD Treat the SSD as camera original media. Test the exact drive, cable, firmware, power setup, and recording mode. VariCam internal recording expressP2, P2, microP2, plus possible SD proxy media depending on model and setup Professional master, sub-recorder, dailies, and proxy workflows Preserve the full P2 structure. Plan for Panasonic drivers, P2-aware viewing, and metadata-safe offload. VariCam PURE V-RAW Codex Capture Drive with Codex V-RAW recorder Uncompressed 4K RAW workflows up to the supported frame rates Use Codex handling, offload, preview, and dailies tools. Do not treat the media like a generic USB SSD. For most production teams, the rule is simple: use USB-SSD recording when the camera explicitly supports it for the format you need, when the drive is on the camera vendor’s confirmed list or your team has tested it at your exact settings, and when your data workflow can treat removable drives as camera originals. If any of those are uncertain, build the day around the camera’s native media and use SSDs for verified offload instead. Match the media to the Panasonic camera family Panasonic’s current LUMIX USB-SSD workflow is meant to solve a specific problem: some codecs and frame sizes generate more data than SD cards can reasonably support, or aren't recordable to SD at all. Panasonic notes, for example, that GH7 can record 5.7K 30p ProRes RAW HQ in-camera, but not to SD card. On cameras that support USB-SSD recording, the SSD becomes the recording destination for those heavier modes. The important compatibility constraints are concrete. Panasonic’s GH6 support notes say external SSD recording requires firmware version 2.2 or later , uses SuperSpeed USB 10Gbps, and supports USB Type-C SSDs up to 2 TB. Panasonic also recommends using SSDs whose operation has been confirmed by Panasonic, while making clear that this isn't a guarantee for every condition or every unit. That wording matters because “USB-C SSD” isn't a single performance class. A tiny portable drive, an NVMe blade in an enclosure, and a bus-powered rugged SSD may all mount on a computer, but behave differently on a camera powered from a small battery, hanging off a rig, recording long takes in heat. For LUMIX USB-SSD recording, treat these as minimum expectations: Camera firmware supports USB-SSD recording for that body SSD capacity is within the camera’s supported limit, commonly up to 2 TB on documented models such as GH6 Drive and cable support the required USB generation, such as USB 3.2 Gen 2 / 10Gbps where specified The specific recording mode is allowed to record to SSD You have formatted the drive in the camera before production use Your team has tested the exact drive, cable, power setup, and record mode in a long-form test The last line is the one that saves shoots because a drive that records a 20-second test clip may still fail during a long interview, high frame rate take, or hot exterior day. Don't mix up USB-SSD with P2 and Codex workflows On the professional cinema side, Panasonic workflows are built around different media assumptions. VariCam 35 records to expressP2, P2, and microP2 media depending on configuration. Its main recorder supports formats including AVC-Intra 4K, AVC-Intra 2K, AVC-Intra 100/200, and multiple ProRes options. Your team can use the sub recorder for lower-resolution or proxy-style media, depending on the setup. VariCam 35 also supports simultaneous recording of a master and dailies , plus in-camera color grading where CDL and 3D LUT information can be stored with main and sub recordings. That media management feature means editorial can receive lighter material quickly while the finishing path keeps the camera originals intact. VariCam PURE is different again because V-RAW recording uses a Codex V-RAW 2.0 Recorder and Codex Capture Drive media. Panasonic describes this as uncompressed 4K RAW up to 120 fps, with offload, preview, and dailies handled through Codex workflow tools. If the show is shooting V-RAW, plan for Codex media handling from the start. Don't assume the DIT can pull a commodity USB SSD and copy it like a LUMIX drive. P2 workflows also have computer-side requirements. Panasonic notes that a PC needs the included P2 driver to recognize , copy, and transfer P2 files, and P2 Viewer Plus or compatible editing software may be required for preview. That affects offload stations, editorial machines, and any “just plug it in” expectations. Set the camera mode before formatting and testing media Select the recording mode before media testing. The drive that works for 4K LongG may not be appropriate for ProRes, RAW, high frame rate, or open gate recording. On VariCam, settings such as frequency, main pixel, main codec, and high speed govern Panasonic’s system operation. Changing frequency can require a restart. VariCam LT similarly separates resolution, codec, frame rate, SDI RAW output, VFR, and proxy behavior. In other words, the camera isn't simply “in 4K.” It's in a full system mode that controls which media paths and recording options are valid. For LUMIX USB-SSD work, the same production logic applies even if the menus look simpler. Decide these settings first: Container and codec, such as MOV, ProRes, ProRes RAW, or another supported mode Resolution and sensor area, such as UHD, DCI, open gate, or cropped modes Frame rate and whether the mode is normal, high frame rate, or S&Q Bit depth and chroma sampling where selectable Audio requirements Monitoring LUT versus baked-in look Whether cards, proxies, or external recorders are part of the same workflow Some Panasonic models disable features when USB-SSD mode is enabled. G9II documentation notes that when USB-SSD is set to on , recording to cards and playback of card media are unavailable, double card slot functions are unavailable, and certain USB, firmware update, and copy functions are unavailable. It also notes power requirements for some higher-frame-rate video modes, including use of an AC adaptor and DC coupler for specified conditions. USB-SSD changes the camera’s operating state, which means camera assistants, DITs, and post supervisors need to know what becomes unavailable when SSD recording is enabled. Format in the camera and keep the media identity stable Format camera-original media in the camera that will record it. That applies whether the “media” is a LUMIX USB-SSD, a P2 card, or a Codex Capture Drive. Computer formatting can create the wrong file system, allocation behavior, partition layout, or hidden file clutter, and it may mount fine on a laptop and still behave badly in-camera. A sane formatting workflow starts with a controlled naming system. The physical label, camera reel, volume name, and offload folder should agree as closely as possible. If the camera doesn't allow custom volume names, use your own drive labels and offload folder names to preserve the identity. A practical reel naming pattern might include: Camera letter, such as A, B, or C Shooting day, such as D01 Media index, such as 001, 002, 003 Optional project code for multi-show environments For example, a physical SSD label might read A_D01_003 . The offload folder should carry the same identity. If the camera writes a different internal volume name, record that in the camera report or media log. The goal is that nobody has to guess whether “Untitled,” “NO NAME,” or “SSD_1” is the same drive as the one in the shot log. A stable media identity should follow the SSD from camera use through offload. Before the shoot, format each SSD in-camera, record a test clip in the final production mode, power-cycle the camera, and play the clip back from the camera. Then offload that test clip through the same ingest station that your team will use on set. This catches three categories of problems early: the camera can't sustain the mode, the computer can't read the media as expected, or the folder structure isn't what editorial expects. Choose recording modes around the post path The right Panasonic recording mode is the one that preserves the creative intent while keeping the rest of the pipeline honest. For color-managed work, V-Log/V-Gamut is usually about keeping latitude for post rather than making the on-set image look pretty. Panasonic describes V-Log as having characteristics similar to a film scan log curve, designed to preserve exposure information for grading. That means your team needs to plan monitoring separately from recording. A LUT on a monitor or proxy can help the director, DP, and editor see intent without forcing that look into the master. VariCam workflows make this explicit. You can select V-Log, V-709, or graded views for sub-recorder, EVF, LCD, and external monitor output, depending on configuration. Panasonic’s LUT guidance also cautions that your team generally shouldn't bake a LUT into the master because it restricts adjustment in post. Applying a LUT to monitoring or proxy files is often useful. Burning a LUT into originals is a finishing decision. For editorial speed, simultaneous master and sub/proxy recording can be more valuable than raw bandwidth. VariCam 35 can record a master and dailies at the same time. VariCam LT has related master and proxy capabilities depending on configuration. If the show needs fast dailies, make sure your team tests file names, timecode, clip metadata, and LUT handling before the first shoot day. Matching proxy and master names determines how painless conform will be later. For LUMIX SSD shoots, where the SSD may hold the only high-quality original, decide whether editorial will cut from those originals, transcodes, or proxies. If editors are remote, don't wait until wrap to discover that a day’s worth of ProRes RAW or high-bitrate MOV files need to be transcoded before anyone can view them. Rig the SSD like camera media The most common USB-SSD failures are boring: bad cable, stressed connector, unsecured drive, accidental unplug, overheated drive, or power behavior that your team never tested. Mount a production SSD so the cable can't wiggle at the camera port. Short certified cables are usually safer than long flexible ones, but only if they don't put side-load on the USB-C connector. Cage clamps, SSD mounts, and right-angle adapters can help, but every extra adapter is another failure point. Test the final physical build, not just the drive model. A securely mounted SSD and restrained cable reduce the risk of connector movement during recording. Build the rig around these failure modes: Cable bumped during handheld or gimbal work SSD mount blocking heat dissipation Camera battery swap interrupting a recording state Camera assistant removing a drive before recording has fully stopped Same-looking empty and exposed drives mixing in a pouch The access light matters because on Codex and other professional recorders, media status indicators are part of safe handling. On USB-SSD workflows, the camera screen and drive activity indicators are your equivalent. Don't unplug because the tally light stopped. Wait until the camera has fully ended the clip and returned control to the camera operator. Manage multiple SSDs with a reel-based rotation Once SSDs become camera originals, they need the same discipline as camera cards. The DIT or media manager should know which drives are blank, which are exposed, which are copying, which are verified, and which are cleared for reuse. Don't let the camera team and data team invent separate status systems. A simple color or case-position system works well: Blank and formatted media stays in one marked area Exposed media goes into a separate protected area Media being copied stays physically attached to the ingest station The media manager seals or flags verified media after all destinations pass verification Media approved for reuse returns only after the media manager signs it back Avoid erasing or reformatting on camera based only on “I copied it.” Reuse should require verified copies to the agreed number of destinations, plus a readable spot check. If the production requires camera originals to remain untouched until editorial confirms, then your team may need to treat SSDs like mags and hold them for the day or the entire shoot. Capacity planning should account for more than total runtime. Panasonic’s 2 TB guidance on GH6-style USB-SSD workflows means you may need more physical drives than expected for all-day ProRes or RAW recording. Smaller drives can also reduce loss exposure. Losing or damaging one 2 TB drive is worse than one 1 TB drive if your team splits the day cleanly across reels. Preserve the folder structure during offload Copy the entire camera-created volume structure during offload, not just the visible movie files. Panasonic P2 media is especially dependent on its file and metadata structure, and P2-aware tools or drivers may be required. LUMIX SSD folders are more familiar to most NLEs, but the same rule applies: preserve what the camera wrote. A verified offload process should create at least two independent copies before your team reuses media. Many productions use three: primary shuttle, backup shuttle, and nearline or shared storage, and verify at copy time. Verified offload means the camera original is copied to separate destinations and checked before reuse. Use checksum-based copying rather than drag-and-drop. The copy tool should calculate a source hash and destination hash, then report a pass or fail. After that, spot check playback from the destination, not from the original SSD still attached to the camera or reader. If you're dealing with P2, make sure the offload station has the Panasonic driver or compatible software needed to read and preview the files correctly. The media log should capture: Reel or drive ID Camera letter Shoot day First and last clip, if practical Recording format Timecode notes or resets LUT or color pipeline notes Offload destinations Verification result Person responsible for the copy The log needs to be unambiguous when editorial asks, “Where is A camera, day 2, card 7?” Handle split clips and long takes deliberately Some Panasonic recording formats can split long recordings into multiple files or clips while the camera presents them as one continuous take. VariCam documentation notes that P2 recordings may continue automatically as another clip after certain duration thresholds, and that clips may appear as separate clips in nonlinear editing software or on a computer. AJ-PX270 documentation also includes file split options such as one file, split, and short split depending on recording format and media. This isn't necessarily a problem, but it's a conform risk if someone copies only part of the media or renames files manually. Long interviews, concerts, lectures, and live events are where this shows up most often. For long-form recording days, warn editorial that split files may be normal. Offload whole volumes. Avoid manual renaming inside camera folders. If your team transcodes, confirm that the transcode tool joins or interprets spanned clips correctly, and keep the originals intact until picture lock and final conform are safe. The setup that usually works For a LUMIX USB-SSD shoot, the clean setup is a current firmware body, a Panasonic-confirmed or production-tested USB-C SSD within the supported capacity limit, a short reliable cable, in-camera formatting, and a record test at the exact delivery mode. Use USB-SSD when the format needs it or because the workflow benefits from direct-to-drive capture. For VariCam, separate the master, proxy, LUT, and RAW decisions early. If you record internally, plan around P2 or expressP2 behavior and required computer drivers. If you record V-RAW, plan around Codex media and Codex offload. Use simultaneous master and dailies when it helps editorial, but test naming and conform before production. For every Panasonic workflow, the media rule is the same: the recording format decides the media, the media decides the offload plan, and the offload plan decides when anything can be erased. If your team makes those three decisions in that order, SSD recording becomes a production advantage instead of a data management gamble. FAQ No. Use USB-SSD recording only on Panasonic cameras that explicitly support it, with firmware that enables the feature, and with a drive that meets the camera’s capacity and USB speed requirements. For example, GH6 support notes specify firmware 2.2 or later, SuperSpeed USB 10Gbps, and SSDs up to 2 TB. Panasonic also recommends using SSDs whose operation has been confirmed, but that still doesn't replace testing the exact drive, cable, power setup, and recording mode before production. Format camera-original media in the camera that will record it. Computer formatting can create file system, partition, or hidden-file issues that may not be obvious until recording. After formatting, record a test clip in the final production mode, power-cycle the camera, play the clip back in-camera, and offload it through the same ingest station that will be used on set. No. LUMIX USB-SSD recording, P2 or expressP2 recording, and Codex-based VariCam RAW recording are different workflows. LUMIX bodies such as GH6, GH7, G9II, and S5IIX-style setups may support direct USB-SSD recording for certain high-bitrate modes. VariCam systems more commonly use P2, expressP2, microP2, proxy media, or external RAW systems. VariCam PURE V-RAW uses Codex Capture Drive media, not generic USB-C SSDs. The selected codec, resolution, frame rate, RAW or ProRes mode, bit depth, and proxy behavior determine whether a drive and camera configuration are valid. A drive that works for a lower-bitrate 4K mode may fail or be unsupported for ProRes, RAW, high frame rate, or open gate recording. Testing should always be done at the exact settings planned for the shoot. Treat SSDs as camera originals, not accessories. Use a clear reel or drive ID system that connects the physical label, camera report, offload folder, and media log. Keep blank, exposed, copying, verified, and reusable media physically separated. Don't erase or reformat a drive until the agreed number of checksum-verified copies has been made and the media manager has released it for reuse. Preserve the full camera folder structure, but don't rely on folder names alone for the production record. Add fields for camera letter, shoot day, reel ID, recording format, LUT intent, copy destination, and verification status so assistants and post supervisors can find the right media later with custom metadata.

title: HR Reporting Standardization: The Essential Guide for Multi-Unit Businesses in 2026
summary: Learn how multi-unit businesses can standardize HR reporting in 2026, improve data consistency, and enable faster, more informed workforce decisions.
body_text: What is HR Reporting Standardization and Why Multi-Unit Businesses Need It Defining HR reporting standardization HR reporting standardization establishes uniform formats, structures, and definitions for employee-related data across systems, departments, and reporting environments. This process captures and maintains workforce information—such as job titles, cost centers, compensation elements, and employee identifiers—consistently across all locations. Standardization creates a single source of truth for HR data at its core. Organizations develop predefined formats for names, IDs, departments, and roles when they implement hr data standards, along with unified coding structures for cost centers, payroll, and job classifications. Data dictionaries provide central definitions for each element. Validation rules enforce standardized inputs across the organization. The International Organization for Standardization has formalized this approach through ISO 30414 , which provides guidance and requirements for organizations to measure, report, and disclose human capital outcomes. This standard helps organizations learn about risks and chances for eco-friendly growth, whatever their size or sector. HR reporting itself is the backbone of any data-driven team, with predefined, routine data outputs collected weekly, monthly, or quarterly and pulled directly from HRIS, ATS, and payroll systems. Standard hr reports deliver core operational metrics that managers and senior leaders require. These metrics appear in HR dashboards and get exported in formats like CSV and PDF files for audit reports or government submissions. The multi-unit business reporting challenge Managing workforce compliance becomes more challenging by a lot when businesses expand across multiple locations. Different branches often follow different attendance practices, separate approval methods, and varying reporting standards. Inconsistent compliance processes across locations create one of the biggest obstacles HR teams face. This fragmentation makes centralized control nearly impossible. HR teams struggle with several critical issues during multi-location operations. Poor visibility creates serious workforce compliance problems because teams cannot monitor operations immediately. Many organizations still rely on spreadsheets, emails, and manual processes for workforce compliance management. These cause data duplication, reporting inconsistencies, missed updates, and delayed approvals. Attendance management becomes nowhere near as simple in multi-location operations. HR teams face attendance discrepancies, delayed attendance reports, and lack of immediate attendance visibility. These attendance compliance issues directly affect payroll accuracy and overall workforce compliance management. Communication delays compound these challenges. Compliance actions get delayed when workforce updates are not shared properly between branches and HR teams. Workforce data becomes inconsistent, and reporting accuracy decreases. Each branch or operational unit may have different workforce requirements—different shifts and varying operational schedules—making it difficult to maintain consistent employee compliance tracking. HR teams struggle with collecting location-wise data and verifying workforce records without centralized systems. Generating accurate reports across multiple locations can be time-consuming. This administrative burden reduces overall efficiency and creates more workforce compliance challenges. Benefits of standardized HR data Organizations with mature standardization processes see improved operational efficiency and stronger compliance management when they implement hr reporting strategy through standardization. Better decision-making capabilities follow. Consistent reporting creates a single source of truth, which is vital for all aspects of HR data analysis. Verified and standardized datasets make insights both strategic and trusted. Only 10% of organizations directly link workforce data to business in a meaningful, systemic way. This reveals a significant chance for those who implement proper standardization. Standardized data makes accurate reporting, continuous system integration, and improved decision-making possible by eliminating inconsistencies and ambiguity in workforce data. Organizations can provide cohesion and reduce mistakes. Employees get a consistent experience whatever their location. Centralized workforce data helps HR teams access immediate workforce information and improve reporting visibility. Data inconsistencies decrease. This centralization improves operational control by a lot. Immediate HR reporting allows managers to have presence in attendance data, whether an employee is working, on leave, or working overtime. Teams can address attendance issues before they become major problems with this visibility. Standardization supports planning by helping uncover trends and make forecasts that are essential for informed decisions and organizational growth. HR can use these insights to line up workforce planning with long-term business objectives. The right talent to meet future challenges gets secured. Standardized processes help improve consistency and reduce operational confusion for multi-location companies. Compliance tracking becomes simpler. Cross-business-unit reporting becomes feasible when all locations follow the same data standards and protocols. Platforms like inFeedo can support this consistency by providing unified frameworks for collecting and analyzing HR data insights across dispersed teams. SaaS HR reporting platforms make scalability possible for growing businesses. These systems easily scale to support business growth as companies open new branches or hire more employees. Existing HR processes remain undisrupted. HR data integration across multiple systems—HRIS, payroll platforms, and ERP systems—lines up to a single standardized structure. Uniformity gets maintained over time. Common HR Reporting Challenges in Multi-Unit Organizations Multi-unit organizations face a distinct set of obstacles when managing workforce data across dispersed locations. These challenges create ripple effects that touch every aspect of HR operations, from daily attendance tracking to annual compliance audits. Inconsistent data collection across locations Different branches often develop their own methods for capturing employee information. This creates a patchwork of data standards that rarely line up. One location might record job titles as "Store Manager" while another uses "Retail Manager" for the similar role. Cost centers get coded differently. Employee IDs follow separate numbering systems, and department names vary across sites. These discrepancies result from human error during data entry and format differences across systems. Missing or incomplete data fields add to the problem. Employees or administrators transpose numbers, misspell names, or enter information in unauthorized formats. The errors compound across multiple locations. Data left blank during entry or transfer creates gaps that affect calculated fields and exclude employee information from subsequent analyzes. Cross-module inconsistencies emerge when data is siloed across separate systems with different formats and standards. An employee's given name in one system might appear as a nickname in another. Their married name shows up in payroll while their birth name remains in benefits records. This fragmentation makes establishing a single source of truth nearly impossible. Lack of up-to-the-minute HR reporting visibility Research shows that fewer than 25% of companies can employ collected data to produce even simple insights into employee deployment and management. As many as 92% of organizations cannot download and combine data from multiple automated systems to generate meaningful metrics for reports and dashboards. The scope of this problem extends beyond simple inconvenience. HR professionals use an average of 6.17 HCM providers and face barriers to unified reporting. Among these professionals, 77% store data across multiple HCM databases. Another 71% cannot transfer or share that data across databases. Delayed visibility prevents managers from monitoring workforce activity in the moment. Attendance data, productivity metrics, and staffing levels remain locked in individual location systems. Decision-makers lack the immediate insights they just need to address operational issues. By the time weekly or monthly reports surface problems, the chance for timely intervention has passed. Manual processes and data silos Disconnected systems force HR teams into repetitive manual work that consumes time and introduces errors. A single manual data entry carries an estimated cost, and tasks like recording tax form information or verifying timecard accuracy cost even more. Over half of SMEs spend one full day per week on admin-heavy HR tasks. This translates to 416 hours per person annually. Data silos prevent information from flowing between recruiting, onboarding, payroll, and performance management systems. When these platforms don't communicate naturally, HR teams manually transfer employee data between them. This process opens the door to costly mistakes. A single misplaced number or missed update guides to payroll errors and compliance issues. What adds to the complexity is that 80% of HR and payroll professionals report that disparate or duplicate data makes creating accurate reports difficult. Spreadsheets and email chains become shadow tools that organizations employ to bridge gaps between disconnected systems. These workarounds provide no guarantee of accuracy or security. Multi-location operations face a particular challenge when generating reports. They must collect data from each site, verify records manually, and consolidate information into a unified format. This administrative burden reduces efficiency and creates bottlenecks that slow down initiatives. Compliance and regulatory risks Inaccurate or incomplete data creates substantial compliance exposure. Organizations handle sensitive employee information that includes Social Security numbers, family status, bank account details, and medical claims. They face serious consequences when errors occur during data entry, processing, or sharing. Wrong information might misrepresent employees or end up in unauthorized hands if incorrect contact details are stored. Employee master data drives legal and regulatory reporting. Gaps in tax information, expired work permits, or missing job descriptions open organizations to non-compliance risks and reputation damage. Clean data becomes the only protection against these threats. Audit readiness suffers when HR systems cannot produce complete and consistent records on demand. Compliance auditors flag missing work authorization data that disjointed systems never reported. Organizations scramble to gather documentation reactively. An average of 1 in 5 payrolls contains errors, with typical issues costing amounts to fix. Beyond corrections, 14% of companies face payroll litigation annually and receive an average of 32 legal complaints each year. Platforms like inFeedo help organizations maintain consistent HR data across locations. They reduce these compliance risks through unified data collection and reporting frameworks that ensure regulatory requirements are met systematically rather than reactively. Essential Standard HR Reports Every Multi-Unit Business Must Track Six core report categories are the foundations of effective HR reporting standardization for multi-unit operations. Each serves a distinct purpose to maintain workforce visibility, ensure compliance, and support strategic decisions across locations. Workforce metrics and headcount reports Headcount reporting provides an accurate understanding of the total number of people in an organization at any given time. It enables categorization based on quantitative and qualitative information. A typical headcount report has job status (active or inactive), job title, schedule status (part-time, full-time, contract), time in role, salary, exemption status, age, gender, ethnicity, education level, location, retirement age, and veteran status. Measuring headcount matters by a lot for mid-to-large-sized organizations with hundreds or thousands of employees. This data provides the base for workforce planning decisions and helps avoid overstaffing, achieve optimal headcount, and potentially reduce labor costs while maximizing overall HR strategy efficiency. Organizations with more than 100 employees must perform demographic reporting under Equal Employment Opportunity Commission guidelines. This demonstrates clear efforts to vary their workforce. Calculating headcount requires defining consistent employee classification across all units accurately. A full-time employee working 40 hours per week counts as one worker. A part-time employee working 20 hours per week counts as half a worker. Temporary workers or contractors should be considered separately because they lack the same long-term cost commitment as permanent staff. Turnover and retention analytics Employee turnover data analysis collects data, analyzes, and reports HR data to understand a company's turnover rate. Breaking turnover data down provides insights into who is leaving, when most employees depart, and which demographic groups leave more often. Distinguishing between voluntary and involuntary turnover gives a more accurate picture of organizational health. Voluntary turnover occurs when workers leave by their own choice and is more expensive typically. It mainly involves the loss of better performers. Involuntary turnover happens when companies terminate employees, which can be positive (policy violations) or negative (layoffs that indicate financial difficulties). Turnover costs US businesses as much as $1 trillion annually in voluntary turnover alone. Estimates suggest losing a worker can cost a company up to 1.5-2x the worker's salary. Translating turnover data into monetary value helps convey urgency to company leadership about retention issues. Compensation and payroll reports Payroll reports are detailed documents that summarize employee compensation, taxes, deductions, and contributions for specific pay periods. Key components have gross pay (total compensation before deductions that has simple salary, allowances, overtime, bonuses), net pay (take-home salary after deductions), statutory deductions (Professional Tax, TDS, EPF, ESI), and employer contributions. Employers in India must file Form 24Q quarterly , which has details of salary paid to employees and tax deducted at source. This form consists of two annexures. Annexure I is required for all four quarters and Annexure II is needed only in the final quarter. Time and attendance tracking Attendance reports record and track working hours and overtime hours effectively. These reports visualize the number of employees present, absent, and on duty. They also show employees who check in early or late, time spent on breaks and actual working hours, employees who work overtime, and working days of each employee. Monitoring leave trends closely allows quick identification of alarming increases or decreases. Increases could suggest teams aren't balancing leave enough. Sharp decreases could precede burnout. Both situations affect organizational productivity. Performance management reports Performance reports provide objective foundations to evaluate employees and give overviews of how each employee progresses toward goals. They highlight skills, positive and negative feedback received, and overall appraisal scores. Key performance indicators measure progress toward defined business goals. title: What is Earned Wage Access and How Does It Work?
summary: Learn how Earned Wage Access (EWA) works, its benefits for employees and employers, and why more businesses are adopting on-demand pay solutions to support financial wellness and workforce retention.
body_text: We live in a world with instant access – rides on demand, groceries and even cars delivered at your doorstep. But what happens when rent or mortgage is due on Friday and payday isn’t until next Tuesday? Not long ago employees might have been negotiating with their landlord or lender or turning to risky stopgap options to bridge the gap. Today, a newer workplace benefit called earned wage access (EWA) is changing that dynamic. EWA allows employees to access a portion of the wages they’ve already earned on demand, rather than waiting for the traditional pay cycle to catch up with real life. According to 2025 data from the Federal Reserve System , 37% of adults say they could not cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or cash equivalents. No surprise, EWA is increasingly viewed as both a helpful tool for unexpected expenses and a competitive workforce benefit with over 55 million workers now having access to earned wage solutions . For employers, it can support recruiting and retention efforts . For employees, it can offer more control over their financial life and help ease stress between pay cycles . Wage Access Ahead of Payday With employer-sponsored EWA, workers receive income for work they’ve already performed, ahead of payday. The amount they’ve received prior to payday is then deducted or paid directly from their regular paycheck. There are no credit checks, and no interest is charged. Some employer-sponsored EWA programs are free for employees, while others charge an optional flat fee for expedited access, such as an instant transfer. Still, the cost is minimal compared to the steep, compounding interest common with other loans. Some other loans can be short-term, high-interest loans that typically must be repaid in full on the borrower’s next payday. With an average annual interest rate that can exceed those of a typical credit card , borrowers who cannot repay end up in a cycle of debt. EWA, however, allows employees to access wages they’ve already earned without taking on expensive debt. While it’s not a substitute for every situation, and not all workers have access to EWA, it can reduce reliance on high-cost options for employees who need financial flexibility between paychecks. The Benefits of EWA Benefits of EWA for Employees Benefits of EWA for Employers Cover Unexpected Expenses EWA gives employees the ability to withdraw money they’ve already earned when an unexpected expense or emergency arises. Improved Employee Retention Financial support programs can strengthen retention by helping employees feel more secure and valued in the workplace. Mitigate the Need for High Interest Loans Employees can access their wages without having to potentially pay steep interest rates or fall into unsustainable debt cycles. Reduced Turnover Costs Replacing an employee can cost money in recruiting and lost productivity, so offering a benefit like EWA can quickly pay for itself. More Financial Control On-demand, earned income helps employees better manage their cash flow, which can reduce financial stress. Competitive Hiring Advantage More workers are becoming aware of EWA, so offering it can help employers stand out when attracting candidates. Greater Paycheck Flexibility Employees gain control over when they get paid, making it easier to align their earnings with their actual needs. Increased Employee Engagement If employees experience less financial stress at home, that can translate to greater focus, performance, and contentment at work. Why Earned Wage Access Is Gaining Traction Today’s workforce expects greater flexibility and visibility into their compensation, including the timing of their pay. Employers, in turn, increasingly recognize that financial stress doesn’t stay at home. It follows employees to work and can impact focus, attendance, and engagement. That’s why employers, especially those operating in tight labor markets, have come to see EWA as a valuable financial wellness benefit that can help them attract and retain high-performing candidates. The rise of embedded finance has accelerated this shift. Advances in digital payroll infrastructure have made it easier for businesses to integrate EWA into their existing systems. It’s becoming clear that digital payroll transformation isn’t just good for employees; it’s good for business. Partnering with Pathward Offering earned wage access starts with the right partner.
