In assessing the overall health of the business during the three and nine months ended June 30, 2026 and 2025, our management has either included or excluded the following items in general categories, each of which is described below. Adjusted EBITDA. Adjusted EBITDA is defined as net income attributable to Cerence Inc. before net income (loss) attributable to income tax (benefit) expense, other income (expense) items, net, depreciation and amortization expense, and excluding amortization of acquired intangible assets, stock-based compensation, and restructuring and other costs, net and impairment charges related to fixed and intangible assets and gains or losses on the sale of long-lived assets, if any. From time to time we may exclude from Adjusted EBITDA the impact of events, gains, losses or other charges that affect the period-to-period comparability of our operating performance. Other income (expense) items, net include interest expense, interest income, and other income (expense), net (as stated in our Condensed Consolidated Statement of Operations). Our management and Board of Directors use this financial measure to evaluate our operating performance. It is also a significant performance measure in our annual incentive compensation programs. Restructuring and other costs, net. Restructuring and other costs, net include restructuring expenses as well as other charges that are unusual in nature, are the result of unplanned events, and arise outside the ordinary course of our business such as employee severance costs, consulting costs relating to our transformation initiatives, and costs for consolidating duplicate facilities. Amortization of acquired intangible assets. We exclude the amortization of acquired intangible assets from non-GAAP expense and income measures. These amounts are inconsistent in amount and frequency and are significantly impacted by the timing and size of acquisitions. Providing a supplemental measure which excludes these charges allows management and investors to evaluate results “as-if” the acquired intangible assets had been developed internally rather than acquired and, therefore, provides a supplemental measure of performance in which our acquired intellectual property is treated in a comparable manner to our internally developed intellectual property. Although we exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets from our non-GAAP expenses, we believe that it is important for investors to understand that such intangible assets contribute to revenue generation. Amortization of intangible assets that relate to past acquisitions will recur in future periods until such intangible assets have been fully amortized. Future acquisitions may result in the amortization of additional intangible assets. Stock-based compensation. Because of varying valuation methodologies, subjective assumptions and the variety of award types, we exclude stock-based compensation from our operating results. We evaluate performance both with and without these measures because compensation expense related to stock-based compensation is typically non-cash and awards granted are influenced by the Company’s stock price and other factors such as volatility that are beyond our control. The expense related to stock-based awards is generally not controllable in the short-term and can vary significantly based on the timing, size and nature of awards granted. As such, we do not include such charges in operating plans. Stock-based compensation will continue in future periods. Other expenses. We exclude certain other expenses that result from unplanned events outside the ordinary course of continuing operations, in order to measure operating performance and current and future liquidity both with and without these expenses. By providing this information, we believe management and the users of the financial statements are better able to understand the financial results of what we consider to be our organic, continuing operations. Included in these expenses are items such as other charges (credits), net (gains) losses from extinguishment of debt, net (gains) losses from foreign currency translation, and changes in indemnification assets corresponding with the release of pre-spin liabilities for uncertain tax positions. Non-GAAP total operating expenses. Non-GAAP total operating expenses reflect GAAP operating expenses excluding stock-based compensation, intangible asset amortization, and restructuring and other costs. Our management and Board of Directors use this financial measure to evaluate our operating performance. It is also a significant performance measure in our annual incentive compensation programs. Key Performance Indicators We believe that providing key performance indicators (“KPIs”) allows investors to gain insight into the way management views the performance of the business. We further believe that providing KPIs allows investors to better understand information used by management to evaluate and measure such performance. KPIs should not be considered superior to, or a substitute for, operating results prepared in accordance with GAAP. In assessing the performance of the business during the three months ended June 30, 2026, our management has reviewed the following KPIs, each of which is described below: Percent of worldwide auto production with Cerence Technology (TTM): The number of Cerence enabled cars shipped on a TTM basis as compared to IHS Markit car production data. Change in number of Cerence connected cars shipped: The year-over-year change in the number of cars shipped with Cerence connected solutions. Amounts calculated on a TTM basis. Change in Adjusted total billings YoY (TTM): The year over year change in total billings excluding Professional Services and fixed license billings and adjusted for fixed license consumption. Amounts calculated on a TTM over prior year TTM basis. ____________ See the tables at the end of this press release for non-GAAP reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. To learn more about Cerence AI, visit www.cerence.ai , and follow the company on LinkedIn . About Cerence Inc. Cerence Inc. (NASDAQ: CRNC) is a global industry leader in creating intuitive, seamless, AI-powered experiences across automotive and transportation. Leveraging decades of innovation and expertise in voice, generative AI, and large language models, Cerence powers integrated experiences that create safer, more connected, and more enjoyable journeys for drivers and passengers alike. With more than 525 million cars shipped with Cerence technology, the company partners with leading automakers, transportation OEMs, and technology companies to advance the next generation of user experiences. Cerence is headquartered in Burlington, Massachusetts, with operations globally and a worldwide team dedicated to pushing the boundaries of AI innovation. For more information, visit www.cerence.ai . title: Pega Named a Leader in AI Platforms by Independent Research Firm
summary: Pega’s AI-powered platform recognized for agent and app development capabilities, with Pega Blueprint excelling in workflow design
body_text: Press Releases Pega Named a Leader in AI Platforms by Independent Research Firm Pega’s AI-powered platform recognized for agent and app development capabilities, with Pega Blueprint excelling in workflow design Waltham, Mass. – August 6, 2026 – Pegasystems Inc. (NASDAQ: PEGA), the enterprise AI software company for mission-critical work, today announced Forrester Research named Pega a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: AI Platforms, Q3 2026 (1). Pega received the highest scores possible in eight of the 19 total evaluation criteria. The report explains, “Pegasystems offers a comprehensive AI Platform with roots in workflow automation, customer offer personalization using machine learning, and sophisticated decisioning,” and goes on to state that “Pegasystems’ mantra of “Design for people, build for change” extends to helping global enterprises build AI apps that assist employees and customers as well as automate complex, regulated business workflows.” Forrester’s evaluation explains, “Pegasystems’ agent and app development tools excel, especially for workflows via its Blueprint capability,” and notes that Pega customers “appreciate the platform’s ease of use for technical developers and business users alike in creating hybrid workflows that combine business processes with agents.” The report’s profile on Pega concludes that “Pegasystems is a good fit for customers that wish to implement complex, regulated workflows using AI agents.” Pega was among the 15 most significant AI platform providers evaluated and received the highest scores possible in the Current Offering criteria of agent development, AppGen tools, cohesive experience, and governance controls. It also received the highest scores possible in the Strategy criteria of innovation, roadmap, partner ecosystem, and community. Forrester evaluated Pega Infinity™ , Pega’s AI suite of products designed to help enterprises scale AI with confidence. The evaluation included Pega Platform™ , Pega’s application development platform for designing, automating, and optimizing business workflows that improve efficiency and customer experiences, and Pega Customer Decision Hub™ , Pega’s AI-powered decisioning platform that delivers next-best actions to personalize customer engagement at scale. The report also evaluated Pega Blueprint AI™ , Pega’s design agent that transforms operational insights into agentic workflows. This report is among Pega's recent analyst recognition for its enterprise AI and automation capabilities. Pega was recognized as a Leader in the Gartner® Magic Quadrant for Process Intelligence Platforms (2), The Forrester Wave™: Real-Time Interaction Management Software (RTIMS), Q4 2025 report (3), the Gartner® Magic Quadrant for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies (4), The Forrester Wave™ for Digital Process Automation, Q3 2025 report (5), the Gartner® Magic Quadrant for Process Mining Platforms 2025 (6), and a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: AI Decisioning Platforms, Q2 2025 (7). For more background and additional analyst reports, visit www.pega.com/analyst-reports . Quotes & Commentary: “As organizations continue to invest in AI, many are still seeking effective ways to orchestrate AI across people, systems, and workflows to deliver measurable business outcomes,” said Kerim Akgonul, chief product officer, Pega. “We believe this recognition from Forrester further validates Pega’s approach to enterprise AI. By bringing together governance, AI, workflow automation, and decisioning in a single platform, Pega enables organizations to move from AI design to execution faster and with confidence, while its no per-token pricing model helps ensure predictable outcomes, predictable costs, and maximum business value.” Supporting Resources: Report complimentary access: The Forrester Wave™: AI Platforms, Q3 2026 title: $41.7M U.S. Navy Contract to Scale Multi-MW KARNO Power Modules
summary: Hyliion’s largest military contract to date: $41.7 million U.S. Navy award to design, develop, and deliver two multi-megawatt KARNO Power Modules
body_text: Hyliion’s largest military contract to date: $41.7 million U.S. Navy award to design, develop, and deliver two multi-megawatt KARNO Power Modules Deepening Navy Partnership: This award brings Hyliion’s cumulative ONR funding to more than $58 million, spanning initial validation, testing, upcoming at sea trials, and now multi-megawatt development Built for military missions: KARNO technology’s fuel-flexible operation, high efficiency, and low-maintenance design are the attributes driving continued Navy investment in the platform AUSTIN, Texas– Hyliion Holdings Corp . (NYSE American: HYLN), a developer of modular power plant technology, today announced it has been awarded a $41.7 million contract from the Office of Naval Research (ONR) to design, develop, and deliver two multi-megawatt KARNO ™ Power Modules for validation in land and maritime applications at NAVSEA, Philadelphia. This contract represents Hyliion’s largest military contract to date and marks a significant milestone in scaling the KARNO platform toward multi-megawatt power solutions for both defense and commercial applications. Under the contract, Hyliion will develop and deliver two KARNO Power Modules rated at 2+ MW and 3+ MW scale, expanding the platform to support a broader range of U.S. Navy vessels and applications. These systems build on the company’s modular 800 kW architecture to meet the higher power requirements of naval and land-based missions. “This contract accelerates the development of our multi-megawatt KARNO systems and expands the range of naval platforms the technology can support,” said Thomas Healy, Founder and CEO of Hyliion. “The Office of Naval Research has been a tremendous partner in advancing the KARNO technology, and their continued investment reflects the confidence they have built in both our team and the platform.” The multi-megawatt KARNO Power Modules are expected to expand the capabilities that have driven Navy interest in the technology: unmatched fuel flexibility, high electrical efficiency, and a low-maintenance design optimized for demanding operating environments. These attributes can reduce logistical burden, extend mission endurance, and deliver resilient power for maritime and expeditionary operations while maintaining low acoustic and thermal signatures. This award underscores the critical role of investment in accelerating innovative power technologies that support national security and the domestic industrial base. It also validates Hyliion’s strategy of deploying a common KARNO architecture across diverse markets, enabling the same scalable platform to serve both defense missions and high-growth distributed power applications including data centers. The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official policy or position of the Department of Defense or the U.S. Government. About Hyliion Hyliion is committed to creating innovative solutions that enable clean, flexible and affordable electricity production. The Company’s primary focus is to provide modular power plant technology that can operate on various fuel sources to future-proof against an ever-changing energy economy. Headquartered in Austin, Texas, and with research and development in Cincinnati, Ohio, Hyliion is initially targeting the commercial and waste management industries with a locally deployable KARNO Power Module that can offer prime power as well as energy arbitrage opportunities. Beyond stationary power, Hyliion will address mobile applications such as vehicles and marine vessels. The Company aims to offer innovative, yet practical solutions that contribute positively to the environment in the energy economy. For further information, please visit www.hyliion.com. body_text: CHIMERA INVESTMENT CORPORATION'S SECOND QUARTER EARNINGS MAINTAIN SUPPORT FOR $0.45 DIVIDEND August 05, 2026 6:45 am EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio Presentation PDF NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Chimera Investment Corporation (NYSE: CIM) today announced its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Business Highlights: Maintained dividend coverage and strong liquidity position. Spread movements and changes in interest rates impacted book value. Generated Earnings Available for Distribution from both Investment Portfolio and Residential Origination segments. Investment Portfolio Segment Completed two re-securitizations of residential mortgage loans with an aggregate principal balance of $487 million. Purchased an additional $122 million of newly originated loans from HomeXpress, bringing loans retained at quarter end to $301 million. Advanced plans for the inaugural securitization using HomeXpress collateral, which serves to integrate both segments. Residential Origination Segment Originated volume of $1.1 billion, up 30% vs prior year period1, demonstrating platform scale and capacity. Generated $9 million of net income and $12 million of EBTDA, representing an annualized EBTDA ROE of 17.3%2. Product mix shifted, with consumer Non-QM representing 47%, Investor Loans 48%, and QM at 5%. “Chimera delivered resilient second quarter results amidst continued macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty, scaling our loan origination business, and redeploying capital toward higher-return opportunities,” said Phillip J. Kardis II, President and CEO. “Earnings available for distribution were $0.46 per share for the second quarter and $1.00 for the first half of the year, supporting the $0.45 quarterly dividend. As we enter the second half, we remain focused on disciplined execution and sustaining dividend coverage over the course of the year.” ____________________ 1 Reflects HomeXpress standalone results. HomeXpress was acquired on October 1, 2025 and is not included in Chimera’s consolidated results prior to that date. 2 EBTDA ROE, or return on equity, represents the EBTDA divided by Chimera's initial capital investment of $272 million, annualized. Non-cash imputed compensation expense reflects the portion of the consideration paid in the Palisades Acquisition that pursuant to the sellers’ contractual arrangements is distributable to the sellers’ legacy employees (who are now our employees) and that for GAAP purposes is recorded as non-cash imputed compensation expense with an offsetting entry recorded as a non-cash contribution from a related party to stockholders’ equity. The excluded amounts do not include any normal, recurring compensation paid to our employees. Transaction expenses are primarily comprised of costs only incurred at the time of execution of our securitizations, certain structured secured financing agreements, and business combination transactions, and include costs such as underwriting fees, legal fees, diligence fees, accounting fees, bank fees, and other similar transaction-related expenses. These costs are incurred prior to or at the execution of the transaction and do not recur thereafter. Recurring expenses, such as servicing fees, custodial fees, trustee fees, and other similar ongoing fees, are not excluded from EAD. We believe that excluding these costs is useful to investors because it is generally consistent with the treatment applied by our peer group in their non-GAAP measure presentations, mitigates period to period comparability issues tied to the timing of securitization and structured finance transactions, and is consistent with the accounting for the deferral of debt issuance costs prior to the fair value election option made by us. We also believe it is important for investors to review EAD as it is consistent with how management internally evaluates the performance of the Company. Stock compensation expense charges incurred on awards to retirement eligible employees is reflected as an expense over a vesting period (generally 36 months) rather than reported as an immediate expense. We may hold long and/or short positions in TBA securities through transactions commonly referred to as “dollar roll” transactions. Under U.S. GAAP, these transactions are accounted for as derivatives and are carried at fair value. Changes in the fair value of TBA positions consist of two components: (i) drop income (expense) and (ii) mark-to-market adjustments. For financial statement presentation purposes, drop income (expense) is reported within Periodic interest on derivatives, net, while mark-to-market adjustments are reported within Net unrealized gains (losses) on derivatives. Together with any realized gains and losses, these amounts are included in Net gains (losses) on derivatives in our Consolidated Statements of Operations. Management includes drop income (expense) in EAD because it views drop income (expense) as the economic equivalent of net interest income on the underlying Agency securities, reflecting the difference between the implied interest earned and the implied financing cost over the period from trade date to settlement date. This treatment is consistent with how management evaluates the Company’s investment performance and how we believe our investors analyze our investment performance. We view EAD as one measure of our investment portfolio's ability to generate income for distribution to common stockholders. EAD is one of the metrics, but not the exclusive metric, that our Board of Directors considers when determining the amount, if any, of dividends on our common stock. Other metrics that our Board of Directors may consider when determining the amount, if any, of dividends on our common stock include, among others, REIT taxable income, dividend yield, book value, cash generated from the portfolio, reinvestment opportunities, and other cash needs. To maintain our qualification as a REIT, U.S. federal income tax law generally requires that we distribute at least 90% of our REIT taxable income (subject to certain adjustments) annually. EAD is different from REIT taxable income. For example, differences between EAD and REIT taxable income may result from whether the REIT uses mark-to-market accounting for GAAP purposes, accretion of market discount or OID and amortization of premium, and differences in the treatment of securitizations for GAAP and tax purposes, among other items. Further, REIT taxable income generally does not include earnings of our domestic taxable REIT subsidiaries (“TRSs”) unless such income is distributed from current or accumulated earnings and profits. The determination of whether we have met the requirement to distribute at least 90% of our annual REIT taxable income is not based on EAD, and EAD should not be considered as an indication of our REIT taxable income, a guarantee of our ability to pay dividends, or a proxy for the amount of dividends we may pay. We believe EAD helps us and investors evaluate our financial performance period over period without the impact of certain non-recurring transactions. EAD should not be viewed in isolation and is not a substitute for, or superior to, net income (loss) or net income (loss) per basic share computed in accordance with GAAP. In addition, our methodology for calculating EAD may differ from the methodologies employed by other REITs to calculate the same or similar supplemental performance measures, and accordingly, our EAD may not be comparable to the EAD reported by other REITs. Economic Net Interest Income - Investment Portfolio Segment Economic net interest income of our Investment Portfolio segment is a non-GAAP financial measure that equals GAAP net interest income adjusted for net periodic interest on derivatives, interest income from our Residential Origination segment and interest income from investment in MSR financing receivables, and excludes interest earned on cash and interest expense from our Residential Origination segment. Presenting the net contractual interest payments on interest rate derivatives with the interest paid on interest-bearing liabilities reflects our total contractual interest payments. We believe this presentation is useful to investors because it depicts the economic value of our investment strategy by showing all components of interest expense and net interest income of our investment portfolio. However, Economic net interest income should not be viewed in isolation and is not a substitute for net interest income computed in accordance with GAAP. Where indicated, interest expense, adjusting for any interest earned on cash, is referred to as Economic interest expense. Where indicated, net interest income reflecting net periodic interest on derivatives and any interest earned on cash, is referred to as Economic net interest income. title: Get the Context Your Alerts Are Missing with Event Enrichment by Ariel Russo
summary: This blog post is part of PagerDuty’s ongoing series on how we’re helping customers navigate their journey towards autonomous operations. Read on to learn Event Enrichment automatically pulls context from across your systems (i.e. CMDB) directly into your events, with flexible controls for account-level defaults, service-specific overrides, and team-based access.
body_text: This blog post is part of PagerDuty’s ongoing series on how we’re helping customers navigate their journey towards autonomous operations. Read on to learn about how Event Enrichment builds towards this vision. Every on-call engineer knows the drill. An alert fires. It tells you something is wrong, but not what it means . Is this asset in maintenance? Which team owns it? Is it customer-facing? To find out, you’re off — tabbing between your CMDB, your monitoring tool, a spreadsheet someone maintains “temporarily,” and half a dozen Slack threads. That gap between “an event happened” and “I understand what this event means” is where minutes turn into missed SLAs. Incoming events from monitoring tools typically lack context around infrastructure status, service structure and ownership, and business impact — so responders are left to fill in the gaps manually. The result: slower MTTR, frustrated on-call engineers, and SLAs that quietly slip. Event Enrichment is built to close that gap. Events Without Context Monitoring tools are great at detecting that something changed. They’re not so great at telling you why it matters. They don’t natively know that the server throwing errors is in a scheduled maintenance window, or which team actually owns the failing service, or that this particular alert affects a revenue-critical customer flow. That missing context doesn’t disappear — it just gets pushed onto the human being holding the pager, at 2 am, under pressure. Meet Event Enrichment Event Enrichment, now available for Early Access, automatically pulls context from across your systems (like CMDB data) directly into your events. Account-level defaults, service-specific overrides, and team-based access give you flexible control over exactly what gets added and where. The payoff isn’t just cleaner alerts. In the future, it will give tools like SRE Agent a full, 360-degree view of your environment, so responders spend less time hunting for context and more time actually resolving incidents. How It Works, Under the Hood 1. PagerDuty’s contextual data layer Monitoring tools typically lack context from external systems to which they don’t natively have access. PagerDuty’s contextual data layer solves this by pulling data from systems like ServiceNow CMDB and attaching it directly to events — so third-party latency never delays a notification. Setup starts with schemas : think of each one as your own cached mini-database, with one schema per data source. Load data through a direct ServiceNow integration or CSV-formatted API calls, with more direct integrations on the way. ServiceNow syncs every 12 hours, plus real-time updates for select fields like maintenance status — so you can manage maintenance windows per-event instead of pausing an entire service. 2. Enrichment Rules Once your CDP is configured, you create Event Enrichments — the rules that determine which data gets added to which events. Enrichments can be owned by specific teams, or configured as the account “Default” (one per account) when you need standard enrichment data applied regardless of service ownership. Conditions let you control exactly which events get enriched. You select a schema and the event field it should match against, then define where in Custom Details the matched data lands. 3. Extract and Compose Enrichment rules can do more than attach data — they can also transform it. Using Extract , you can pull a specific value out of a field (for example, using regex to extract a PagerDuty service ID into a standard location so Dynamic Routing can use it). Using Compose , you can build new values out of existing ones. And Connect Mode lets you build full logic trees that recombine rules, so you’re not duplicating logic across the board. 4. Powering Orchestration Here’s the real unlock: enrichment happens before orchestration. That means Orchestration can act on data that was never in the original event. If ServiceNow says an asset is in maintenance, the alert gets suppressed automatically — no noise, no page. Events route automatically to the owning team based on enriched data, so you can finally retire the giant hard-coded routing table. 5. Seeing It in Action Trigger an event, and you’ll see it enriched in real time — for example, with enriched_infra and enriched_service fields populated straight from the contextual data layer. That enriched data is what suppresses the noisy, in-maintenance alert and routes the real one to the correct service, even when the monitoring tool itself didn’t have the right service mapping. The Bigger Picture: Fueling Autonomous Operations Event Enrichment standardizes and enriches inbound signals to unlock better correlation, routing, and automation. In turn, that will give features like SRE Agent a clearer understanding of service and infrastructure relationships — and a 360-degree view it can use to make smarter recommendations for resolving incidents. That’s the data flywheel effect: every incident becomes organizational intelligence that helps prevent the next one. Data at scale, intelligent automation, and a system that gets smarter over time — that’s how PagerDuty delivers on Autonomous Operations. See It for Yourself Context shouldn’t be something your team has to go find manually, incident after incident. Event Enrichment brings it to you, automatically, before it’s even needed. Ready to see it in action? Watch the full product demo and sign up for Early Access .

title: Amazon Returns and Recovery Dashboard: How Sellers Can Reduce Returns and Recover Inventory Value
summary: Learn how Amazon's Returns & Recovery Dashboard helps sellers analyze return trends, identify product issues, recover inventory value, and improve profitability.
body_text: In this article, we answer: What the Amazon Returns & Recovery Dashboard is How to use the dashboard to reduce future returns Recovery opportunities for returned inventory Best practices for improving recovery rates Returns are part of selling on Amazon, but they don't have to be a mystery. To help sellers better understand why products are coming back and what can be recovered, Amazon introduced the Returns & Recovery: Insights and Opportunities Dashboard in Seller Central. The dashboard brings together returns data, recovery metrics, customer feedback, and recommended actions into a single view for both Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA) and Fulfilled by Merchant (FBM) orders. Instead of jumping between multiple reports, sellers can now evaluate return trends, identify problem products, and monitor inventory recovery from one centralized location. Why Amazon Created the Dashboard Every returned order has the potential to increase: Shipping costs Processing expenses Inventory losses Disposal costs Customer service time Lost revenue The new dashboard helps sellers move from reacting to returns after they happen to proactively identify patterns that can reduce future return rates. Amazon designed it to surface actionable insights rather than simply reporting historical numbers. Where to Find the Dashboard Eligible sellers can access the dashboard from Seller Central by navigating to: Returns & Recovery → Insights and Opportunities The dashboard is available for both: Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA) Fulfilled by Merchant (FBM) This combined view allows sellers to compare returns across fulfillment methods without switching between multiple reporting tools. What the Dashboard Shows The Returns & Recovery Dashboard combines several types of information that previously lived in separate reports. Returns Performance The dashboard provides an overall picture of return activity, including: Return rate trends Weekly and monthly performance Changes over time High-return products Critical review trends Rather than looking at individual return requests one at a time, sellers can identify broader operational patterns. ASIN-Level Return Analysis One of the most valuable features is product-level reporting. For each ASIN, sellers can review: Return volume Return percentage Most common return reasons Customer feedback Historical trends This makes it easier to identify products that consistently create customer confusion or dissatisfaction. For example, if multiple customers select "Item not as described," it may indicate that the listing needs more accurate images, dimensions, or product details. Return Reasons Amazon groups customer return reasons into categories that help sellers diagnose recurring issues. Common examples include: Arrived damaged Wrong item received Defective product Better price available No longer needed Item different than expected Missing parts Quality concerns Reviewing these trends over time often reveals opportunities to improve product listings, packaging, or quality control. Recovery Insights Returns do not always result in a complete financial loss. The dashboard also highlights opportunities to recover value from returned inventory. Depending on the product's condition and eligibility, Amazon may: Return inventory to sellable stock Grade and resell eligible products Dispose of unsellable inventory Return inventory to the seller For sellers participating in Amazon's Grade and Resell program, the dashboard includes additional recovery metrics such as: Net recovery value Units resold Recovery sales Overall recovery performance These metrics help sellers understand how much value is being recovered instead of written off as a loss. Related Reading: FBA Returnless Resolutions Actionable Recommendations Unlike traditional reporting tools, the Returns & Recovery Dashboard doesn't simply display data. Amazon also surfaces recommendations based on return patterns. Examples may include: Improve listing images Clarify sizing information Update product descriptions Review packaging methods Address recurring quality concerns Investigate fulfillment issues These recommendations help sellers prioritize the products likely to have the greatest impact on reducing future returns. Historical Trends Understanding whether returns are increasing or decreasing is often more valuable than reviewing a single week's performance. The dashboard includes historical reporting so sellers can: Compare weekly trends Measure monthly performance Evaluate seasonal changes Monitor improvements after listing updates Identify recurring issues before peak selling seasons Historical reporting makes it easier to determine whether operational changes are actually reducing returns over time. Related Reading: Leveraging Amazon’s Reimbursement Policies: A Comprehensive Guide To Recovering Lost Profits for 1P and 3P How Sellers Can Use the Dashboard The dashboard becomes most valuable when it's incorporated into a regular operational review. Many successful sellers use it to answer questions such as: Which products generate the highest return rates? Are certain return reasons becoming more common? Have recent listing updates reduced returns? Are damaged returns increasing? How much inventory value is being recovered? Which products should be redesigned or repackaged? Rather than treating returns as isolated events, sellers can identify systemic issues that affect profitability across multiple products. Best Practices for Reducing Returns The dashboard identifies problems, but reducing returns requires operational improvements. Many sellers see the greatest impact by focusing on: Improve Product Listings Provide accurate descriptions, dimensions, specifications, and images that clearly set customer expectations. Strengthen Packaging Protect products from damage during transit while ensuring customers receive items in the expected condition. Analyze Customer Feedback Recurring comments often reveal issues before they become widespread return problems. Monitor High-Return ASINs Review products with above-average return rates regularly and investigate the underlying causes. Track Recovery Performance Understand how much inventory is successfully returned to sellable condition and where recoverable value is being lost. Why the Dashboard Matters For many businesses, returns have traditionally been viewed as a customer service issue. Amazon's Returns & Recovery Dashboard reframes returns as an operational metric that can influence inventory management, listing quality, fulfillment performance, and profitability. By combining return analytics with recovery metrics and product-level recommendations, the dashboard gives sellers a clearer picture of where losses occur and where improvements can have the greatest financial impact. Final Thoughts The Amazon Returns & Recovery Dashboard provides sellers with more than a list of returned orders. It serves as a decision-making tool that helps identify why products are being returned, how much value can be recovered, and what actions may reduce future returns. For businesses selling through Amazon, regularly reviewing these insights supports better listing optimization, stronger inventory recovery, and more informed operational decisions. Explore The Supply Chain Source for expert guidance on Amazon returns, reimbursement policies, FBA best practices, inventory management, and other marketplace topics that help sellers reduce costs, improve performance, and stay informed as Amazon's programs continue to evolve.

title: 9 things to know about sales signal tools in 2026
summary: The sales signal tools market has shifted fast. Here are 9 things revenue teams should know before evaluating a tool in 2026.
body_text: Article overview Contact-level resolution is now the baseline, not a differentiator, across credible sales signal tools. Transparent, custom scoring is starting to matter more to buyers than raw "AI-powered" claims. Execution capability, not detection, is where vendors actually differentiate in 2026. The 71% signal-collection-versus-operationalization gap Gartner and Foundry documented hasn't closed just because more tools exist. Introduction The sales signal tools category looked very different two years ago. Back then, having any AI-labeled scoring at all was a differentiator. In 2026, nearly every vendor in the space claims AI-powered detection, which means the meaningful differences have moved elsewhere, into how transparent the scoring is, how deep the execution goes, and how tightly the tool fits into a rep's actual daily workflow inside their CRM and SEP. 1. Contact-level resolution is now table stakes, not a differentiator Where account-level intent alone was once considered sufficient, most credible sales signal tools in 2026 resolve signals down to a named individual, because buying committees are large enough that account-level flags no longer tell a rep who to contact, and buyers have started to notice and ask about this directly during evaluations. 2. Transparent scoring beats black-box AI As more tools claim "AI-powered" scoring, the ones that show their work, the specific signals behind a score, and allow rep override, earn more trust and see higher adoption than opaque models, regardless of underlying sophistication or marketing claims. 3. Custom models built on your own data outperform generic ones A scoring model trained on your own closed-won and closed-lost history reflects what actually predicts a deal at your company. An industry-wide benchmark assumes every company's buyers behave identically, which they don't, and buyers are increasingly asking vendors directly whether the model is customer-specific or shared. 4. Execution is the differentiator, not detection Most vendors can detect a signal. Fewer can turn it into a drafted email or synced ad audience automatically. That execution gap is where evaluation should focus in 2026, not on raw signal detection capability, which has become largely commoditized. 5. Integration depth with Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach, and Salesloft matters most A signal tool that requires reps to leave their existing workflow to see the intelligence tends to see lower adoption over time than one that surfaces insights natively inside the CRM or SEP, no matter how good the underlying signal quality is. 6. The operationalization gap is still wide Gartner research compiled by Foundry found 71% of B2B organizations collect buyer signals, but more than half never operationalize the data, a gap that hasn't closed just because more tools exist in the market claiming to solve it. 7. Modularity reduces switching risk Rather than betting on one all-in-one platform, more revenue teams are adopting modular tools that layer contact-level scoring and execution onto whatever account-level or data infrastructure already exists, reducing the risk of a costly rip-and-replace later. 8. AI adoption in sales and marketing still shows mixed results A 2025 State of AI Adoption in Sales & Marketing study from UserGems and Wynter found only 7% of teams report being "very successful with clear ROI" from AI tools, while 45% report "limited success with uncertain ROI," underscoring why execution and measurable pipeline impact matter more than AI positioning alone. 9. Money-back guarantees are becoming a real trust signal As buyers grow more skeptical of AI-driven ROI claims after several disappointing rollouts, vendors willing to tie pricing to actual pipeline and revenue outcomes stand out from those making unverified promises in a sales deck. What to ask vendors in a 2026 demo Given how much marketing language now overlaps across this category, three questions tend to cut through positioning quickly: can you show me a specific contact, not just an account, that your model would flag right now and explain why; what happens automatically after that contact is flagged, without a human doing anything; and what does your pricing look like once our contact database doubles. Vendors that answer all three concretely, rather than redirecting to a feature list, are the ones worth shortlisting. Where UserGems fits UserGems is the AI command center for outbound and ABM, built around contact-level scoring, transparency, and automatic execution into the tools revenue teams already use. It's modular, backed by a custom scoring model built on your own sales history, and tied to a money-back guarantee based on pipeline and revenue. FAQ What's changed most about sales signal tools going into 2026? The shift from account-level detection to contact-level resolution paired with automatic execution, rather than tools that simply surface more data. Why does scoring transparency matter so much? Because reps and marketers won't act consistently on a score they can't understand or verify, no matter how accurate the underlying model claims to be. Is AI adoption in sales and marketing actually delivering ROI? Results are mixed. A 2025 UserGems and Wynter study found only 7% of teams report clear ROI, while 45% report limited or uncertain success, which is why execution and measurable outcomes matter more than AI branding. What's the single best question to ask a vendor to cut through 2026's AI marketing noise? Ask what happens automatically after a contact is flagged, without any human action, since that's where most vendors' claims start to diverge from reality. ‍ No items found. No items found. title: 8 Best AI IVR Solutions for Insurance in 2026
summary: 8 IVR platforms compared on telephony, compliance, voice quality, and pricing for insurance. See which fits your carrier, MGA, or agency.
body_text: Insurance calls are rarely simple. Customers call to check claim status, understand coverage, make payments, update policy details, report an incident, or speak with someone about a problem that may already be stressful. Traditional IVR systems handle these conversations by asking callers to navigate menus: “Press 1 for claims, press 2 for billing.” That works for predictable requests, but it becomes frustrating when the customer's issue does not fit neatly into the menu. AI-powered IVR takes a different approach. Instead of forcing callers through a fixed decision tree, an AI voice agent can understand what the customer is asking, collect information, complete routine tasks, and bring in a human when the conversation needs one. In this guide, we compare legacy and AI-powered IVR for insurance across six practical factors, so you can decide which approach makes more sense for your contact center in 2026. TL;DR Plivo is a strong all-round option for insurers that want AI voice, telephony, routing, and digital channels closer together. Vapi is best for developer-led teams that want maximum flexibility across models, telephony, and backend integrations. Retell AI works well for teams that want to add conversational AI on top of existing telephony without rebuilding everything. Bland AI is a good fit for high-volume insurance automation across claims, servicing, and outbound workflows. Synthflow AI suits ops-led teams that want a more no-code way to manage structured insurance conversations. ElevenLabs stands out when natural voice quality is especially important for sensitive policyholder calls. Twilio is a strong choice for enterprises that want a highly customizable IVR and communications stack. LiveKit is best for engineering teams building a more custom voice and telephony architecture. For insurers moving beyond rigid phone menus, Plivo is one of the more balanced options to evaluate because it brings AI voice and the communications layer closer together without forcing the setup across as many separate systems. Why Insurance Companies Are Replacing Legacy IVR Legacy IVR still works for simple tasks, but insurance contact centers are starting to hit its limits. The problem is not that menus are always bad. It is that insurance conversations are often too varied, too contextual, and too sensitive to fit neatly into a fixed “press 1, press 2” structure. Customers may call about a claim, a payment, a policy change, an accident, a renewal, or something they do not know how to categorize. When the IVR forces them to choose the wrong path, the call usually ends up taking longer or getting transferred anyway. AI-powered IVR gives insurers more flexibility. Instead of making the customer navigate the system, the system can identify intent, collect the right information, pull approved data from backend tools, and decide whether the request can be handled automatically or needs a human. The bigger reason insurers are making the shift is operational. A more conversational system can reduce unnecessary transfers, simplify complex call flows, and make it easier to update workflows without rebuilding large decision trees every time a product, process, or customer journey changes. That does not mean legacy IVR is disappearing completely. For highly predictable actions or simple authentication steps, fixed menus can still be useful. The change is that insurers are increasingly using AI for the parts of the conversation where rigid menus create more friction than value. What Actually Matters When Evaluating IVR Solutions for Insurance A good insurance IVR has to do more than sound impressive in a demo. Once it goes live, it needs to handle sensitive conversations, connect with core systems, route calls reliably, and give teams enough control to manage quality over time. 1. Telephony Ownership and Latency The voice experience depends heavily on the phone network underneath it. If the AI layer and telephony sit across multiple vendors, you add more systems to manage and more places where delays or failures can happen. That matters on calls like FNOL, where a policyholder may already be stressed and even small pauses can make the conversation feel awkward. 2. Enterprise Compliance Insurance teams usually have stricter security and governance requirements than a typical customer-support operation. Depending on the workflow and region, buyers may need to evaluate areas like SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, data residency, encryption, access controls, and AI governance requirements before a platform ever reaches production. 3. Code + No-Code Builder Access Claims and operations teams understand the customer journey, but they should not need engineering support every time a call flow changes. At the same time, developers still need APIs and deeper control for integrations with policy, claims, CRM, or payment systems. The strongest platforms give both teams a way to work without forcing everything through one interface. 4. Voice Quality Insurance calls can be emotional. Customers may be reporting an accident, questioning a denied claim, or trying to understand a billing issue. Voice quality is not just about choosing a realistic voice. Turn-taking, pacing, interruptions, background noise, and how naturally the agent responds all affect whether the interaction feels trustworthy. 5. Omnichannel Support A policyholder may start with a phone call and continue the conversation over SMS, WhatsApp, or chat. If every channel sits in a separate system, context gets lost quickly. Platforms that can keep more of the customer journey connected make it easier to avoid repeated questions and fragmented service. 6. Post-Deployment Quality Tooling Getting the agent live is only the beginning. Insurance teams need a way to test edge cases, review real conversations, score agent behavior, spot failed workflows, and catch compliance issues before they become bigger problems. Simulation, evaluations, analytics, and debugging tools matter just as much as the initial builder once the system is handling real policyholders. IVR Solutions for Insurance Compared on 6 Factors Tool Telephony Ownership and Latency Enterprise Compliance Code + No-Code Voice Quality Omnichannel Post-Deployment Quality Tooling Plivo Native telephony, fewer layers in the call path Yes Yes Yes Voice, SMS, WhatsApp, Chat Yes Vapi Usually relies on external telephony providers Yes Developer-first Strong, provider-dependent Voice, SMS, Chat Yes Retell AI Native options + SIP Yes Yes Yes Primarily voice-led Yes Bland AI Bland telephony or BYO SIP/carrier Yes Yes Yes Primarily voice-led Yes Synthflow AI Native telephony + SIP options Yes Strong no-code + API Yes Voice + digital integrations Yes ElevenLabs Usually connects to external telephony Yes Yes Yes Voice, Chat, WhatsApp, SMS, Email Yes Twilio Native telephony infrastructure Yes Developer-first + visual tools Yes Voice, SMS, WhatsApp, Chat Yes LiveKit SIP-based, infrastructure-first Deployment-dependent Developer-first Yes Voice, Text, Video Strong developer observability Plivo Plivo is a strong fit for insurers that want to replace rigid IVR menus with conversational AI without separating the AI layer from the telephony underneath it. Its platform combines built-in telephony and phone numbers with AI agents that can handle voice, SMS, WhatsApp, and chat, which makes it easier to keep more of the policyholder journey in one environment. For insurance teams, that can be useful across workflows like FNOL intake, claims updates, renewals, premium reminders, and policy servicing. The agent can handle routine requests automatically and transfer more complex conversations to a human team when judgment or specialist support is needed. Key Strengths Native telephony: Plivo includes telephony and phone numbers in the same platform as its AI agents, reducing the need for a separate carrier layer. Enterprise compliance: Plivo lists HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2, and PCI DSS support for its platform, which makes it easier to evaluate for regulated insurance workflows. Code + no-code access: Ops teams can build and edit agents through the Vibe Agent experience, while developers can use APIs and deeper integrations for more complex insurance workflows. Omnichannel coverage: The same AI platform can work across voice, SMS, WhatsApp, and chat rather than treating each interaction as a completely separate system. Human escalation: Calls can be transferred to phone numbers, SIP endpoints, agents, or teams when a conversation needs human involvement. Limitations Broader insurance workflows still need integration work: Claims systems, policy platforms, identity verification, and payment systems still need to be connected and governed correctly. The integrated approach may be less appealing to highly modular teams: Insurers that specifically want different vendors for telephony, AI models, transcription, and voice may prefer a more developer-first stack. Pricing Plivo Voice AI Agents cost $0.04 per minute based on the pricing we are using throughout this comparison. Larger deployments can move to Enterprise plans with additional capacity, compliance controls, and global coverage. Vapi Vapi is a good fit for insurers that want to build a more customized AI-powered IVR layer on top of their existing telephony and backend systems. It gives developers control over speech models, call logic, transfers, APIs, and provider choice, which is useful when insurance workflows need to connect to claims systems, policy data, or identity checks. Key Strengths Flexible telephony setup: Vapi can work with external telephony providers and SIP infrastructure, giving insurers more freedom to keep their existing carrier setup. Strong developer control: Teams can customize prompts, tools, routing, transfers, and backend actions around specific insurance workflows. Enterprise compliance support: Vapi supports controls relevant to regulated deployments, including SOC 2, PCI support, SSO, and enterprise access controls. Good voice flexibility: Teams can choose from different voice, transcription, and model providers instead of being locked into a single stack. Strong evaluation tooling: Vapi supports simulations, custom evaluations, transcripts, call artifacts, and post-call analysis, which makes it easier to test and improve IVR behavior over time. Limitations More infrastructure to manage: Because telephony, voice, transcription, and models can come from different providers, insurers may end up with more moving parts in the call path. More engineering-heavy: Claims and operations teams will usually need developer support for deeper integrations and workflow changes. Not a full omnichannel contact-center platform: Vapi is stronger around AI voice and developer flexibility than broader policyholder journey management. Compliance depends on the full stack: Even if Vapi supports enterprise controls, insurers still need to verify how every connected telephony, model, and data provider handles sensitive information. Pricing Vapi charges a $0.05 per minute platform fee, with telephony, transcription, LLM, and voice-provider costs added separately. Depending on the stack, a realistic all-in cost can be around $0.13 to $0.33 per minute. Retell AI Retell AI is a good fit for insurers that want to move beyond fixed IVR menus without rebuilding their entire phone setup. It can sit on top of existing telephony through SIP, handle inbound insurance conversations, connect to backend systems, and transfer more complex calls to human agents with context. Key Strengths Works with existing telephony: Insurers can connect Retell through SIP instead of replacing their current phone numbers, carrier, or contact-center infrastructure. Strong human handoff: Warm transfers, whisper messages, and three-way introductions make it easier to move claims, disputes, or sensitive conversations to the right human team. Good voice experience: Retell is built around real-time conversational voice, making it a stronger replacement for rigid menu-based IVR when callers need to explain an issue naturally. Enterprise compliance: Retell supports requirements including SOC 2, HIPAA, and GDPR, which makes it more relevant for regulated insurance environments. Post-deployment QA: Its monitoring and AI QA capabilities help teams review latency, hallucinations, knowledge accuracy, sentiment, and other issues once the agent is handling real policyholder calls. Limitations Telephony is not always fully consolidated: If insurers use their own SIP or carrier setup, Retell becomes another layer rather than replacing the whole voice stack. Some transfer capabilities depend on configuration: Certain custom telephony setups can affect how native transfer features work. Insurance workflows still need backend integration: Claims systems, policy administration, authentication, and payment workflows have to be connected separately. More AI-first than omnichannel-first: Retell is strongest around voice automation, so insurers looking for one platform across voice, SMS, WhatsApp, and broader digital servicing may want a more integrated communications stack. Pricing Retell AI costs $0.07 to $0.31 per minute, depending on the voice, model, telephony, and configuration used. Bland AI Bland AI is a good fit for insurers that want to automate a larger share of claims, servicing, and inbound support calls without staying tied to rigid phone trees. It has a dedicated insurance offering for workflows like claims intake, quoting, policy servicing, and lead qualification, and it can connect into existing telephony or contact-center infrastructure when teams do not want to replace everything at once. Key Strengths Insurance-specific workflows: Bland explicitly supports claims intake, policy servicing, quoting, and other insurance call flows rather than positioning itself only as a generic voice agent. Enterprise compliance: Bland publishes support for controls including SOC 2 Type II and PCI DSS, which makes it more relevant for regulated insurance environments. Flexible telephony: Enterprise teams can use Bland's telephony or connect their own SIP infrastructure, which helps if an insurer wants to keep an existing carrier or contact-center setup. Warm human handoff: Bland supports warm transfers so the AI agent can brief the human agent before the policyholder is connected. Built for higher-volume automation: Bland is positioned around large-scale inbound and outbound voice automation, which can suit insurers handling large volumes of repetitive claims or servicing calls. Limitations More AI-first than omnichannel-first: Bland is strongest around voice-led automation, so insurers looking for one tightly integrated platform across voice, SMS, WhatsApp, and broader digital servicing may need additional systems. Some deeper capabilities are Enterprise-only: SIP connectivity and several advanced transfer and infrastructure options are tied to Enterprise deployments. Insurance workflows still need careful governance: Claims decisions, required disclosures, authentication, and escalation rules still need to be designed around the insurer's own policies and regulatory requirements. The broader contact-center layer may still sit elsewhere: Human-agent desktops, workforce management, and other traditional CCaaS functions may still require another platform. Pricing Keeping the pricing used in this comparison, Bland AI starts at $0.14 per minute, with larger deployments moving to higher-volume or Enterprise arrangements based on capacity, telephony, and infrastructure needs. Synthflow AI Synthflow AI is a good fit for insurers that want to move away from rigid IVR trees without making every workflow change an engineering project. Its no-code builder is useful for claims and operations teams, while SIP connectivity, call transfers, APIs, and structured flows give technical teams enough control for more complex insurance journeys. Synthflow also explicitly positions its voice AI for financial services and insurance use cases such as caller verification, claims processing, and account requests. Key Strengths No-code + developer flexibility: Ops teams can build and adjust workflows visually, while developers can use APIs and integrations for deeper claims or policy-system connections. Enterprise compliance: Synthflow lists SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 among its supported compliance standards. Human handoff options: It supports warm and cold transfers, including whisper messages or summaries before a human agent takes over. Useful data controls: Teams can configure data retention and PII redaction at the agent level, which is helpful for insurance workflows involving sensitive customer information. Strong testing and QA: Synthflow supports simulations and custom evaluations, giving teams a way to test edge cases and score agent behavior before and after launch. Limitations Telephony can still involve multiple systems: More complex deployments may use SIP trunks, PBX systems, or existing CCaaS platforms alongside Synthflow. Advanced setups need technical work: The agent builder is no-code, but integrations with policy systems, claims platforms, and enterprise telephony can still require engineering support. PII protection still needs oversight: Automated redaction and retention controls help, but insurers still need their own governance around what data the agent can access, store, or pass downstream. Not a full insurance platform: Claims decisions, underwriting logic, authentication, and policy administration still need to live in approved backend systems. Pricing Synthflow uses pay-as-you-go pricing for self-serve usage, with larger insurance deployments moving to Enterprise pricing based on call volume, concurrency, telephony, integrations, and compliance requirements. ElevenLabs ElevenLabs is a good fit for insurers that care heavily about how natural the conversation feels, especially for sensitive calls like claims, billing disputes, renewals, or policy questions. ElevenAgents now goes well beyond voice generation, with insurance-specific workflows, SIP connectivity, human transfers, guardrails, simulations, and post-call evaluations that make it more practical as an AI-powered IVR replacement. Key Strengths Excellent voice quality: ElevenLabs remains one of the strongest options when natural pacing, tone, and conversational delivery are a priority. Insurance-specific workflows: Its current insurance offering covers use cases such as claims intake, policy questions, renewals, payment reminders, and status updates. Strong compliance baseline: ElevenAgents lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI DSS Level 1, HIPAA, GDPR, Zero Retention Mode, and regional data residency options. Human escalation: Calls can be transferred to external phone numbers or SIP destinations when a policyholder needs a human agent. Strong testing and evaluation tooling: Teams can run simulated conversations, define evaluation criteria, and review production performance before and after deployment. Limitations Telephony may remain separate: ElevenLabs commonly connects through SIP or other telephony integrations, so the full voice stack may still involve another provider. Not a full insurance contact-center platform: Claims administration, policy systems, workforce management, and other core operations still need to live elsewhere. Natural voice does not remove workflow complexity: Authentication, disclosures, claims rules, and escalation logic still need careful configuration. More infrastructure may be required for complex deployments: Insurers with existing CCaaS, SIP, and backend systems will still need integration work to make the whole journey feel seamless. Pricing Keeping the pricing used in this comparison, ElevenLabs starts at $6 per month, with higher usage, telephony, and other production costs added as the deployment scales. Twilio Twilio is a strong fit for insurers that want to build a highly customized IVR or conversational voice experience on top of established telephony infrastructure. Its Programmable Voice stack supports traditional IVR, AI-based self-service, routing, payments, and integrations, while tools like ConversationRelay and Dialogflow CX integrations give teams a path toward more conversational experiences. Key Strengths Native telephony infrastructure: Twilio handles phone numbers, calling, routing, and programmable voice directly, which gives insurers more control over the call path. Flexible IVR architecture: Teams can build anything from a simple menu-based IVR to a more conversational AI workflow using Programmable Voice, Studio, and AI integrations. PCI-compliant payment workflows: Twilio supports PCI Mode for Programmable Voice, including workflows designed to securely capture and redact payment-card information. Omnichannel coverage: Twilio supports voice alongside SMS, WhatsApp, chat, and email, which is useful when policyholder journeys continue beyond the phone call. Strong monitoring and analytics: Voice Insights and related contact-center tooling give teams visibility into call performance and operational issues once the IVR is live. Limitations More engineering-heavy: Twilio gives insurers a lot of flexibility, but building and maintaining more advanced AI-powered IVR workflows typically requires technical resources. AI capabilities are spread across products: Programmable Voice, Studio, Flex, ConversationRelay, Dialogflow CX integrations, and analytics can all form part of the final setup, so the architecture can become complex. Compliance varies by product: Not every Twilio AI feature is eligible for HIPAA or PCI-sensitive workflows. For example, Twilio currently states that Flex Agent Copilot is not HIPAA eligible or PCI compliant. Can be more platform than some insurers need: Teams looking for a simpler way to replace a legacy IVR with a conversational agent may prefer a more packaged AI voice platform. Pricing Keeping the pricing approach used throughout this comparison, Twilio is pay as you go. Voice, phone numbers, AI services, call recording, and other components are generally billed separately depending on the configuration. LiveKit LiveKit is a good fit for insurers with strong engineering teams that want to build a highly customized AI-powered IVR rather than adopt a more packaged system. It provides the real-time voice infrastructure, SIP connectivity, transfers, and agent framework, while leaving more of the workflow design and insurance-specific logic in the hands of the team building on top of it. Key Strengths Strong telephony flexibility: LiveKit supports SIP-based inbound and outbound calling, DTMF, secure trunking, and both cold and warm transfers, which gives insurers a solid foundation for replacing traditional IVR flows. Good voice infrastructure: HD voice, noise cancellation, secure media transport, and real-time communication tooling make it well suited to teams that care about call quality at the infrastructure level. Human escalation: Warm transfers can pass context to a human agent and handle transfer failures more gracefully than a simple call forward. Useful compliance controls: LiveKit publishes SOC 2 Type II and GDPR support, along with region pinning and encrypted SIP media. HIPAA-eligible services are also available under the appropriate agreement. Deep developer control: Teams can build custom routing, integrations, agent logic, and policyholder workflows instead of being limited to a predefined IVR builder. Limitations Developer-first: LiveKit gives teams flexibility, but claims or contact-center ops teams will usually need engineering support to build and change production workflows. Telephony can involve another provider: SIP deployments may still require an external trunking provider, so the final setup can have more infrastructure layers than a platform with fully integrated telephony. Not insurance-specific out of the box: Claims intake, policy servicing, authentication, disclosures, and other insurance logic still need to be designed and integrated by the customer. Compliance depends on the architecture: LiveKit provides useful security and regional controls, but insurers still need to validate the full stack, including carriers, AI providers, storage, and backend integrations. Pricing Keeping the pricing used throughout this comparison, LiveKit starts at $50 per month, with additional usage-based costs depending on telephony, agents, inference, recordings, and the rest of the infrastructure used. Choosing the Right IVR Solution for Insurance The right choice usually comes down to how complex your policyholder conversations are, how much control your team needs, and whether you want to replace the legacy IVR completely or modernize it in stages. For insurers that want AI + telephony in one stack Plivo is a strong option if you want telephony, routing, AI voice, and omnichannel communication closer together. That can simplify workflows like FNOL intake, claims updates, premium reminders, and policy servicing without adding as many separate vendors to the call path. For developer-led teams that want maximum flexibility Vapi works well when your engineering team wants control over models, telephony, APIs, and call logic. It is a good fit for insurers building more customized workflows around existing claims, policy, or verification systems. For teams that want faster AI-IVR deployment Retell AI is a good middle ground between flexibility and ease of rollout. It works well for insurers that want to layer conversational AI onto existing telephony while keeping transfers, monitoring, and QA relatively straightforward. For high-volume insurance automation Bland AI makes sense when the goal is to automate a large number of repetitive insurance calls across claims intake, policy servicing, quoting, or outbound follow-ups. It is especially relevant when AI is expected to handle a meaningful share of the conversation before a human steps in. For ops teams that want a no-code approach Synthflow AI is a better fit when claims or contact-center teams need to update workflows without depending on engineering for every change. Its visual builder makes it easier to manage structured insurance journeys while still allowing deeper integrations when needed. For insurers where voice quality matters most ElevenLabs stands out when the conversation itself needs to feel especially natural. That can matter in claims or sensitive service calls where tone, pacing, and responsiveness affect how comfortable the policyholder feels. For enterprises that want a highly customizable platform Twilio is a strong choice if you already use its communications stack or have the engineering resources to build around it. It can support everything from traditional IVR to more conversational AI workflows, but the final setup may span several Twilio products. For engineering teams building a custom IVR stack LiveKit is best suited to insurers that want infrastructure-level control over voice, SIP, routing, agents, and integrations. It offers a lot of flexibility, but more of the insurance-specific workflow and governance layer has to be built by your team. The main decision is whether you want to keep extending a legacy IVR, add an AI layer on top of your existing setup, or move toward a more integrated conversational platform. For teams starting fresh, Plivo is one of the more balanced options to evaluate because it brings telephony, AI voice, routing, and digital channels closer together without forcing the whole workflow across multiple vendors. Final Thoughts Legacy IVR still has a place in insurance, especially for simple and predictable tasks. But once policyholder conversations involve claims, billing issues, renewals, verification, or more emotional situations, fixed menus start to show their limits. AI-powered IVR gives insurers more flexibility, but the best platform is the one that balances that flexibility with telephony reliability, compliance, human handoff, and strong post-launch monitoring. Vapi and LiveKit suit more technical teams, Retell and Bland work well for AI-led automation, Synthflow is easier for ops teams, and ElevenLabs stands out for voice quality. For insurers that want to modernize without adding too many separate systems, Plivo is one of the more practical options to evaluate because it keeps telephony, AI voice, routing, and digital channels closer together. Want to modernize your insurance IVR without adding more complexity? If your team is looking to move beyond rigid phone menus and bring AI voice, telephony, routing, and customer communication into a more connected setup, Plivo is worth putting on your shortlist. Bloomin’ Brands, Inc. is one of the largest full-service dining restaurant companies in the world with a portfolio of leading, differentiated restaurant concepts. The Company’s restaurant portfolio includes Outback Steakhouse, Carrabba’s Italian Grill, Bonefish Grill and Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar. The Company owns, operates and franchises more than 1,440 restaurants in 46 states, Guam and 12 countries. For more information, please visit www.bloominbrands.com . Non-GAAP Measures In addition to the results provided in accordance with GAAP, this press release and related tables include certain non-GAAP measures, which present operating results on an adjusted basis. These are supplemental measures of performance that are not required by or presented in accordance with GAAP and include: (i) Restaurant-level operating income and the corresponding margin, (ii) Adjusted income from operations and the corresponding margin, (iii) Adjusted segment income from operations and the corresponding margin, (iv) Adjusted net income and (v) Adjusted diluted earnings per share. Restaurant-level operating margin is a non-GAAP financial measure widely regarded in the industry as a useful metric to evaluate restaurant-level operating efficiency and performance of ongoing restaurant-level operations, and we use it for these purposes. We believe that our use of non-GAAP financial measures permits investors to assess the operating performance of our business relative to our performance based on GAAP results and relative to other companies within the restaurant industry by isolating the effects of certain items that may vary from period to period without correlation to core operating performance or that vary widely among similar companies. However, our inclusion of these adjusted measures should not be construed as an indication that our future results will be unaffected by unusual or infrequent items or that the items for which we have made adjustments are unusual or infrequent or will not recur. We believe that the disclosure of these non-GAAP measures is useful to investors as they form part of the basis for how our management team and Board of Directors evaluate our operating performance, allocate resources and administer employee incentive plans. These non-GAAP financial measures are not intended to replace GAAP financial measures, and they are not necessarily standardized or comparable to similarly titled measures used by other companies. We maintain internal guidelines with respect to the types of adjustments we include in our non-GAAP measures. These guidelines endeavor to differentiate between types of gains and expenses that are reflective of our core operations in a period, and those that may vary from period to period without correlation to our core performance in that period. However, implementation of these guidelines necessarily involves the application of judgment, and the treatment of any items not directly addressed by, or changes to, our guidelines will be considered by our disclosure committee.
